origin.text: Escribe una conversación de ocho turnos (unas 190–240 palabras) entre dos compañeros de apartamento. Uno se queja con un mensaje en primera persona y pide un cambio con Would you mind; el otro se disculpa; al menos uno usa wish o if only; y acuerdan una solución.

prompt.es: Escucha el final de la conversación y elige qué actitud muestran los dos.

choices.text: Both accept part of the responsibility and want to repair the relationship.
Only Tom accepts responsibility, while Sara keeps her demand and says nothing more.
Both decide to avoid the subject to keep the peace.

feedback.es: Tom se disculpa y cambia su conducta; Sara reconoce que gritar no estuvo bien: los dos asumen su parte.

origin.audio: Tom listened while Sara explained how she felt. He did not interrupt. When she finished, he said: I'm sorry, Sara. I can see why you are upset. I wish I had noticed earlier. I'll keep the volume low after ten. Sara smiled and answered: Thank you. I'm also sorry that I raised my voice last week. I was tired, but that was no reason to shout.

prompt.es: Completa: «Se puede poner un límite sin atacar: necesito algunas horas de silencio.»

feedback.es: Set a boundary significa poner un límite claro y respetuoso, sin culpar a la otra persona.

origin.text: It is possible to set a ___ without attacking anyone. I do need some quiet hours at night, and I am saying so calmly.

prompt.es: Lee el mensaje de Ana y elige cuál es su postura.

choices.text: She drops her complaint to avoid another argument.
She apologises for her tone but keeps her request.
She blames Leo for the way the rota was designed.

feedback.es: Ana se disculpa por levantar la voz, pero mantiene su petición de cambiar los turnos: disculpa equilibrada.

origin.text: Ana's message to Leo: I know the rota was my idea, and I'm sorry I raised my voice yesterday. Still, I feel tired when I do the dishes three nights in a row. Would you mind swapping with me on Thursdays? I promise to cook on Sundays, because I want us to be fair.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué consigue Mia con su respuesta a las bromas de su compañero.

choices.text: She proves that he has been taking her clothes for weeks.
She accepts his joke and drops the subject for now.
She makes him take the problem seriously without starting a fight.

feedback.es: Mia mantiene la calma, dice cómo se siente y pide algo concreto: él deja de reírse y promete preguntar.

origin.audio: When Mia asked her flatmate to stop borrowing her clothes, he laughed and said it was no big deal. Mia did not shout. She said she felt upset when things disappeared from her room, and she asked him to check first. He stopped laughing and promised to ask.

prompt.es: Lee la situación y elige la disculpa equilibrada que Leo debería decir.

choices.text: I'm sorry I shouted, but I still need some quiet hours at night.
I'm sorry you feel that way, and I will never mention it again.
I apologise, but honestly it was your fault that I raised my voice at all.

feedback.es: La disculpa equilibrada pide perdón por la propia parte y mantiene la necesidad; las otras la retiran o culpan.

origin.text: Leo shouted at his flatmate about the noise last night. Today he wants to apologise without pretending that the problem does not exist. He thinks about what to say.

prompt.es: Completa: «Lo siento, te interrumpí, pero sí necesito terminar mi idea.»

feedback.es: But une la disculpa con la necesidad que se mantiene: pides perdón sin retirar lo que necesitas.

origin.text: Leo wants to apologise without dropping his need. He says: I'm sorry I interrupted you, ___ I do need to finish my point.

prompt.es: ¿Qué frase del mediador resume las dos posturas con equilibrio?

choices.text: Ana needs quiet evenings, but Tom only thinks about his music and his friends.
Tom needs time to practise, so Ana should rest somewhere else.
Ana needs quiet evenings to rest, and Tom needs time to practise.

feedback.es: El resumen equilibrado da a cada persona su necesidad con el mismo peso, sin adjetivos que juzguen.

hint.es: Busca la frase que da a cada uno su necesidad, sin juzgar.

prompt.es: Completa: «Déjame resumir lo que he oído hasta ahora.»

feedback.es: Summarise es resumir; Let me summarise abre un resumen equilibrado antes de proponer una salida.

hint.es: Es el verbo inglés para «resumir»; no es resume.

origin.text: The mediator wants both sides to feel heard before she proposes anything. She says: Let me ___ what I have heard so far.

prompt.es: Ordena: «¿Y si probamos un acuerdo durante dos semanas?»

answer.text: What if we try a compromise for two weeks

feedback.es: What if abre una propuesta sin imponerla; compromise es el acuerdo con cesiones.

hint.es: Empieza por What if y termina con el plazo.

prompt.es: Escucha el relato y elige qué hizo la mediadora antes de proponer una salida.

choices.text: She summarised both positions and pointed out what they shared.
She asked the son to explain why he rarely came home.
She told the mother that her son was right to go out.

feedback.es: La mediadora resume ambas posturas y subraya lo común (querer sentirse respetados) antes de proponer.

origin.audio: In a workshop for volunteer mediators, the trainer described a family argument over Sunday lunches. The mother wanted everyone at the table, while her son wanted time with his friends. The mediator stayed neutral. She summarised both positions, pointing out that they both wanted to feel respected. Then she asked: What if we try a compromise? The son would come twice a month, and the family would choose the dates together. Everyone agreed to review the plan after two months.

prompt.es: Con el mismo relato, elige en qué consistía el compromiso.

choices.text: The son would come every week, but he would leave early after the main dish.
The son would come to lunch twice a month, on dates chosen together.
The mother would stop organising Sunday lunches for good.

feedback.es: El compromiso reparte las cesiones: el hijo viene dos veces al mes y las fechas se eligen entre todos.

origin.audio: In a workshop for volunteer mediators, the trainer described a family argument over Sunday lunches. The mother wanted everyone at the table, while her son wanted time with his friends. The mediator stayed neutral. She summarised both positions, pointing out that they both wanted to feel respected. Then she asked: What if we try a compromise? The son would come twice a month, and the family would choose the dates together. Everyone agreed to review the plan after two months.

prompt.es: Completa: «Un buen mediador no toma partido: ayuda a ambos a encontrar una solución.»

feedback.es: Take sides significa tomar partido por una persona; el mediador se mantiene imparcial.

origin.text: Some people think that a mediator decides who is right. In fact, a good mediator does not ___ sides: she helps both people find a solution.

prompt.es: Escribe el mensaje final de la mediación a Ana y Leo.

answer.text:
Dear Ana and Leo,
Thank you both for talking so openly today. Let me summarise what I heard. Ana, it sounds like you feel overwhelmed when the Sunday plans change at the last minute, and you need to know earlier. Leo, what I'm hearing is that you feel left out when you cannot see your friends, and you need some free time. Neither of you is wrong: you both want a calm weekend and to feel respected.
What if we try a compromise? Leo will tell Ana by Friday evening if he has other plans. Ana will keep Sunday lunch free until then, and she will not ask him to cancel later. If either of you feels upset, please say it with an I-message, for example, I feel frustrated when...
So we agreed that we will follow this plan for two weeks. Let's review it next Sunday, and we can change anything that does not work.
Thank you both for your honesty and your patience. I am proud of how you listened to each other.
Mia

What if we try a compromise? Leo will tell Ana by Friday evening if he has other plans. Ana will keep Sunday lunch free until then, and she will not ask him to cancel later. If either of you feels upset, please say it with an I-message, for example, I feel frustrated when...

Hi Ana and Leo,
I'm glad we talked. To summarise: Ana, it sounds like you feel stressed because the plans for Sunday lunch change suddenly, and you need time to organise. Leo, it sounds like you feel frustrated because you rarely see your friends, and you need space. I think you both want the same thing, which is a peaceful home where everybody feels heard.
Could we agree on a simple solution? Leo will tell Ana by Friday whether he is free on Sunday. In return, Ana will not plan the lunch until she hears from him. If there is a problem, we will speak calmly and take a break first.
So we agreed that this starts this week. We will check in again in two weeks, and then we will decide if we keep it.
Thanks for listening to each other. I'm proud of both of you, and I hope that the plan makes Sundays calmer and happier for everybody in the family. If either of you feels upset before then, please say it with an I-message and we will talk.

feedback.es: Un buen mensaje de mediación resume las dos posturas con equilibrio, reformula emociones, propone una salida y fija el acuerdo y su revisión.

origin.text: Ana se siente agobiada cuando Leo cambia a última hora los planes del domingo y necesita saberlo antes. Leo se siente excluido cuando no puede ver a sus amigos y necesita tiempo libre. Como mediador, escribe un mensaje a los dos (unas 220–270 palabras): resume ambas posturas con equilibrio, reformula sus emociones sin culpar, propone una salida con What if o Could we agree, y fija lo acordado y su revisión.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige por qué la mediadora pregunta a Leo si algo le parece injusto.

choices.text: Because Leo had refused to sign the agreement earlier in the same meeting.
Because she wants to change the plan before it starts.
Because his body language suggests a doubt that he has not voiced.

feedback.es: Leo mira al suelo y duda; la mediadora lo nota y le da espacio para decir lo que no ha dicho.

origin.audio: Ana and Leo had both agreed to the plan, but the mediator noticed that Leo kept looking at the floor. Before closing the meeting she asked him: Is there anything that still feels unfair? Leo hesitated, then said that he would accept the plan, but he was not sure that Ana would keep her side. The mediator wrote that down and suggested a review in two weeks.

prompt.es: Con la misma escena, elige para qué sirve la revisión dentro de dos semanas.

choices.text: To check whether Ana keeps her side and adjust the plan if needed.
To let Leo choose a new plan without talking to Ana about it first.
To decide which of the two people was wrong.

feedback.es: La revisión responde a la duda de Leo: se comprueba el acuerdo y se ajusta si hace falta, sin buscar culpables.

origin.audio: Ana and Leo had both agreed to the plan, but the mediator noticed that Leo kept looking at the floor. Before closing the meeting she asked him: Is there anything that still feels unfair? Leo hesitated, then said that he would accept the plan, but he was not sure that Ana would keep her side. The mediator wrote that down and suggested a review in two weeks.

prompt.es: Completa: «El verdadero punto de fricción es con qué frecuencia come junta la familia.»

feedback.es: Sticking point es el punto de fricción: lo que impide cerrar un acuerdo.

origin.text: Both of them agree on the chores and on the music. The real sticking ___ is how often the family eats together.

prompt.es: Lee el mensaje del mediador y elige qué evita hacer.

choices.text: It avoids blaming Leo, but it asks Ana to give up her Sunday lunch.
It avoids saying which of the two people is to blame.
It avoids naming Ana's feelings, although it describes Leo's clearly.

feedback.es: El mensaje nombra emociones y propone revisar el domingo, pero no dice quién tiene la culpa: mediación imparcial.

origin.text: Hi both, thanks for today. I hear that you both want a calm home. Ana, it sounds like you feel tired when the plans change; Leo, it seems you feel left out. So, could we agree that Leo tells Ana by Friday, and that we review this next Sunday?

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué quiere decir la mediadora con su última frase.

choices.text: That the compromise failed because nobody was happy.
That mediators should make both sides unhappy on purpose, to be fair.
That a fair deal means that each side gives up something.

feedback.es: «Slightly unhappy but respected» resume la idea: en un buen compromiso cada parte cede algo sin perder el respeto.

origin.audio: After two hours of arguing, the brother and sister finally agreed on a plan. Nobody won completely: she gave up her Sunday dinners twice a month, and he promised to call every Friday. The mediator said that a good compromise leaves both people slightly unhappy but respected.

prompt.es: Completa: «Un mediador debe ser imparcial: si toma partido, nadie confiará en ella.»

feedback.es: Impartial describe a quien no favorece a ninguna parte; sin imparcialidad, el mediador pierde la confianza.

origin.text: A mediator must stay ___. If she takes sides, nobody will trust her.

prompt.es: ¿Cuál de estas frases es una instrucción directa del entrenador?

choices.text: Pass the ball sooner and stay in your position.
I love your effort; you never gave up today.
Your strength is your speed, but your passes were late.

feedback.es: La instrucción usa el imperativo (pass, stay) y dice qué hacer ahora; las otras animan o valoran.

hint.es: Busca la frase que empieza con un verbo en imperativo.

prompt.es: Completa: «Tu punto fuerte es tu velocidad, pero tus pases llegaron tarde.»

feedback.es: Strength es el punto fuerte: la retroalimentación útil empieza reconociendo lo que funciona.

hint.es: Es el sustantivo de «punto fuerte»; empieza por str-.

origin.text: The coach did not shout at the team. She simply told Mia: Your ___ is your speed, but your passes were late in the second half.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Sigue así, lo estás haciendo genial bajo presión.»

answer.text: Keep going you are doing great under pressure

feedback.es: Keep going y You are doing great motivan; under pressure cierra la frase.

hint.es: Empieza con Keep going y termina con under pressure.

prompt.es: Escucha la charla del descanso y elige qué función tiene «I love your effort today».

choices.text: It tells her exactly what to change in the second half.
It recognises her effort without giving her an order.
It gives her a fact about how the game is going.

feedback.es: «I love your effort» reconoce el esfuerzo de Mia sin dar órdenes ni datos: es ánimo.

origin.audio: At half-time, the coach spoke to the players. Pass the ball sooner, she told Leo, and stay in your position. Then she turned to Mia. I love your effort today, she said, you never gave up. Your strength is your speed, but your passes were late in the first half, so try looking up before you pass. The team was losing two to nothing, but nobody looked worried. Keep going, the coach added: you are doing great under pressure.

prompt.es: Con la misma charla, elige qué se le pide a Mia que haga distinto.

choices.text: To pass the ball sooner and stay in her position.
To shoot as soon as she sees the space.
To look up before she passes the ball.

feedback.es: La mejora para Mia es mirar antes de pasar; pasar antes y mantener la posición era la instrucción para Leo.

origin.audio: At half-time, the coach spoke to the players. Pass the ball sooner, she told Leo, and stay in your position. Then she turned to Mia. I love your effort today, she said, you never gave up. Your strength is your speed, but your passes were late in the first half, so try looking up before you pass. The team was losing two to nothing, but nobody looked worried. Keep going, the coach added: you are doing great under pressure.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada frase del entrenador con su función.

pairs: Shoot as soon as you see the space.
You never gave up today, well done!
Your passes were late in the second half.

feedback.es: La instrucción dice qué hacer, el ánimo reconoce el esfuerzo y la retroalimentación describe un hecho concreto.

pairs: Shoot as soon as you see the space.
You never gave up today, well done!
Your passes were late in the second half.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué actitud adopta la entrenadora con el jugador.

choices.text: She supports him while giving one clear thing to work on.
She insists that the miss was bad luck and that nothing needs to change.
She praises his courage but avoids saying anything specific about the mistake.

feedback.es: Elogia su valentía y su esfuerzo y señala un único punto concreto: apoyo con una mejora clara.

origin.audio: After the match, the coach sat next to a player who had missed an easy chance. She did not raise her voice. You were brave to try to score, she said, and your effort was the best in the team. The decision was late, though, so next time try looking at the goal before you shoot. Then she smiled. I want you to shoot again on Saturday.

prompt.es: Con el mismo relato, elige por qué dice «I want you to shoot again on Saturday».

choices.text: To give him an order about his new position.
To show that she still trusts him after the mistake.
To warn him that he will be tested on Saturday.

feedback.es: Pedirle que vuelva a disparar demuestra confianza: el fallo no cambia lo que espera de él.

origin.audio: After the match, the coach sat next to a player who had missed an easy chance. She did not raise her voice. You were brave to try to score, she said, and your effort was the best in the team. The decision was late, though, so next time try looking at the goal before you shoot. Then she smiled. I want you to shoot again on Saturday.

prompt.es: Completa: «Prefieren la crítica constructiva: una cosa concreta y un siguiente paso.»

feedback.es: Constructive criticism es la crítica que señala un punto concreto y propone un siguiente paso.

origin.text: Good coaches avoid vague comments like That was bad. They prefer ___ criticism: one concrete thing and a next step.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Levanta la vista antes de pasar el balón.»

answer.text: Look up before you pass the ball

feedback.es: La instrucción va en imperativo y sitúa la condición con before.

prompt.es: Lee el mensaje del entrenador y elige con qué propósito lo escribe.

choices.text: To encourage the team and avoid talking about any mistakes.
To complain that the players do not run enough and to ask for extra running.
To give feedback that recognises a strength and proposes a next step.

feedback.es: El mensaje nombra un punto fuerte (correr), un dato concreto (pérdidas en el medio) y un paso siguiente: retroalimentación.

origin.text: Coach's message to the team: Good work tonight. I know you are tired. Your strength this season is how hard you run, but we lose the ball too often in the middle of the pitch. On Thursday, let's practise short passes. See you at six.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué quiere enseñar el entrenador con sus palabras.

choices.text: That clear, calm instructions help more than shouting does.
That players should never talk during training.
That only the coach is allowed to give instructions.

feedback.es: El entrenador sustituye el grito por frases claras y tranquilas: «Pass to me» en lugar de culpar.

origin.audio: During a training session, a young player kept shouting at his teammates. The coach stopped the practice and said quietly: Encourage, don't blame. When you shout, people get tense and pass the ball too fast. Next time, say what you need: I'm open, or Pass to me. Try it now.

prompt.es: Completa: «Sus comentarios nos mostraron cómo mejorar nuestros pases.»

feedback.es: Improve significa mejorar; la retroalimentación útil enseña en qué y cómo hacerlo.

origin.text: We were losing every game until the coach's comments showed us exactly how we could ___ our passing.

prompt.es: ¿Cuál de estas es una pregunta de coaching abierta, no un consejo ni un sí o no?

choices.text: Do you think you can reach your goal this month?
What would it take to reach a goal this month?
Why don't you just set a smaller goal this month?

feedback.es: Solo «What would it take…?» es abierta: no se responde con sí o no ni esconde un consejo.

hint.es: Descarta la que se responde con sí o no y la que suena a consejo.

prompt.es: Completa: «¿Qué te impide hablar delante del grupo?»

feedback.es: What's stopping you from + -ing busca el obstáculo real que frena a la persona.

hint.es: Es el verbo en -ing que va antes de you from.

origin.text: The player says that she wants to be more confident. Her coach answers with a question instead of advice: What's ___ you from speaking in front of the group?

prompt.es: Ordena: «¿Qué harías si fueras más seguro de ti mismo?»

answer.text: What would you do if you were more confident

feedback.es: La pregunta hipotética une would en la principal con el pasado simple (were) tras if.

hint.es: Empieza con What would you do y usa were tras if.

prompt.es: Escucha la sesión y elige qué hace la entrenadora en lugar de dar un consejo.

choices.text: She explains why mistakes are part of the game.
She warns him that the school team will not wait.
She asks questions that help him name his own problem.

feedback.es: La entrenadora pregunta en vez de aconsejar, y así él mismo nombra su problema (el miedo a equivocarse).

origin.audio: A volunteer coach was talking to a boy who wanted to join the school team but kept finding excuses. She did not tell him to try harder. Instead, she asked: What's stopping you from going to the first training? He said he was afraid of making mistakes in front of the others. So she asked another question: What would it take for you to feel more confident? After a pause he answered that he could ask a friend to come with him. The coach simply smiled.

prompt.es: Con la misma sesión, elige qué sugiere la sonrisa final de la entrenadora.

choices.text: That the idea came from him, which is exactly what she hoped for.
That she thinks his plan is too simple for him.
That she had already decided to invite his friend.

feedback.es: Sonríe porque la solución (llevar a un amigo) la encontró él: es lo que busca una pregunta de coaching.

origin.audio: A volunteer coach was talking to a boy who wanted to join the school team but kept finding excuses. She did not tell him to try harder. Instead, she asked: What's stopping you from going to the first training? He said he was afraid of making mistakes in front of the others. So she asked another question: What would it take for you to feel more confident? After a pause he answered that he could ask a friend to come with him. The coach simply smiled.

prompt.es: Completa: «Es más fácil hallar una solución cuando puedes nombrar el mayor obstáculo.»

feedback.es: Obstacle es lo que se interpone en el camino; nombrarlo es el primer paso de una buena pregunta de coaching.

origin.text: Most people already know part of the answer. It is easier to find a solution once you can name the biggest ___ in your way.

prompt.es: Escribe dos preguntas de coaching para que la jugadora se atreva a pedir ayuda.

answer.text: What's stopping you from asking your coach for help? What would it take for you to feel more confident?
accepted: What's stopping you from asking your coach for help? What would it take for you to feel more confident?
What is stopping you from asking him for help? What would it take to be more confident?
What's stopping you from asking for help? What would it take for you to feel more confident?

feedback.es: Dos preguntas abiertas, una sobre el obstáculo (What's stopping you from...?) y otra hipotética (What would it take...?), sin dar consejos.

origin.text: Una jugadora te dice: «Quiero pedirle ayuda a mi entrenador, pero me cuesta hacerlo.» No le des consejos. Escribe dos preguntas abiertas: una sobre lo que se lo impide (What's stopping you from...) y otra hipotética sobre lo que haría falta para sentirse más segura.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige por qué funcionó mejor el segundo entrenador.

choices.text: The second coach set a more ambitious target than the first coach.
The player found her own solution instead of receiving orders.
The player trusted the second coach more because that coach was more experienced.

feedback.es: La jugadora encuentra su propia solución (usar el descanso); al primero solo le dieron órdenes y no hizo nada.

origin.audio: Two coaches talked to the same player. The first said: You should practise every day, and you should stop worrying. The player nodded but did nothing. The second asked: What would help you to practise three times this week? The player thought for a moment, then said she could use her lunch break. She wrote it down and looked surprised at how simple it was.

prompt.es: Con la misma escena, elige qué sugiere que la jugadora «looked surprised».

choices.text: That she disagreed with the question that the coach had asked.
That she was shocked by how much practice was needed.
That she had not expected to find an answer so easily.

feedback.es: La sorpresa se refiere a lo simple que era la solución, no al desacuerdo ni al esfuerzo requerido.

origin.audio: Two coaches talked to the same player. The first said: You should practise every day, and you should stop worrying. The player nodded but did nothing. The second asked: What would help you to practise three times this week? The player thought for a moment, then said she could use her lunch break. She wrote it down and looked surprised at how simple it was.

prompt.es: Completa: «¿Qué haría falta para hablar con ella?»

feedback.es: What would it take to + verbo es la pregunta abierta que sustituye al consejo disfrazado.

origin.text: Why don't you talk to her? sounds like a question, but it is really advice in disguise. A better version is: What would it ___ to talk to her?

prompt.es: Lee lo que dice el adolescente y elige la respuesta que es una pregunta de coaching.

choices.text: What's stopping you from finishing one small thing this week?
You should finish one small thing every week, starting today.
Why don't you ask a friend to check your work every day?

feedback.es: Solo «What's stopping you…?» es una pregunta abierta; las otras son consejos, aunque una suene a pregunta.

origin.text: A boy tells his coach: I never finish anything, and I do not know why.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige con qué fin hace la entrenadora la segunda pregunta.

choices.text: To reassure the youngest player that there is nothing to be nervous about.
To help the players turn their worry into something useful.
To move the conversation away from winning the match.

feedback.es: La segunda pregunta parte de la emoción de la jugadora y busca convertirla en algo útil, sin juzgarla.

origin.audio: At the end of the session, the coach asked the team: How would you feel if we won the next match? Nobody answered at first. Then the youngest player said that she would feel proud, but also nervous. The coach wrote both words on the board and asked: What would help us turn the nervous feeling into energy?

prompt.es: Completa: «¿Qué opción es más realista esta semana: una sesión larga o tres cortas?»

feedback.es: Realistic describe lo que se puede cumplir en la práctica; una buena pregunta ayuda a elegir una opción realista.

origin.text: You cannot do everything at once. Which option feels more ___ for you this week: one long session or three short ones?

prompt.es: ¿Qué comentario es específico y respetuoso a la vez?

choices.text: You always rush everything you do on the pitch.
That was not very good, but I am sure you will improve.
I noticed that you rushed your last two passes.

feedback.es: Solo el comentario sobre los dos últimos pases cita un hecho concreto sin juzgar a la persona.

hint.es: Busca el que cita un hecho que se vio, sin always ni never.

prompt.es: Completa: «“Estuvo bien, supongo” es un comentario vago: no dice qué repetir.»

feedback.es: Un comentario vago suena amable, pero no cita ningún hecho ni dice qué hacer.

hint.es: Es el adjetivo contrario a specific.

origin.text: That was good, I guess is a ___ comment: it does not tell you what to repeat or what to change.

prompt.es: Ordena: «La próxima vez, respira antes de disparar y mantén la calma.»

answer.text: Next time breathe before you shoot and stay calm

feedback.es: Next time + imperativo es la estructura de un paso accionable.

prompt.es: Escucha los comentarios del entrenador y elige cuál es específico y accionable.

origin.audio: After the tournament, three players received comments from their coach. To the first he said: That was terrible, you never listen. To the second he said: I noticed that you rushed your last two passes, so next time, breathe before you pass and stay calm. To the third he said: That was good, I guess. The third player looked confused and asked: Could you be more specific? The coach thought for a moment and answered: Your talk to the group was helpful because you gave clear examples.

origin.audio: At the volunteer meeting, Sara gave a short presentation. Afterwards, her manager said: That was confusing. Leo, who was sitting next to her, tried again: I noticed that you spoke quickly in the middle, so next time, take a breath before each new idea, and it would help to add one example. Sara nodded.

choices.text: It is vague: it gives an impression but not what to change.
It is disrespectful because it judges Sara as a person, not her presentation.
It is useful because it tells her to explain more.

feedback.es: «Confusing» expresa una impresión sin decir qué cambiar; no ataca a Sara ni propone un paso concreto.

origin.text: Telling someone You need to improve does not help much. A comment is ___ only when it names a step that you can take tomorrow.

prompt.es: Lee el correo y elige qué criterio incumple principalmente.

choices.text: It is vague: it never says how late Tom was.
It is disrespectful: it judges Tom's attitude instead of describing facts.
It is too long and gives Tom several tasks at once.

feedback.es: El correo sí dice cuánto llegó tarde (veinte minutos); lo que falla es que juzga la actitud de Tom.

origin.text: Email to a volunteer: Hi Tom, you were twenty minutes late, again. You clearly do not care about this project. Please fix this.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué da a entender la niña sobre el comentario «Try harder».

choices.text: That it was disrespectful and made her leave the old club at once.
That it was too specific for a player of her age.
That it was vague and did not tell her how to improve.

feedback.es: «Try harder» no dice qué cambiar; el nuevo comentario sí (frenar al final), y por eso le motiva.

origin.audio: A coach told a girl: Your start was fast, but you rushed the final part. Tomorrow, let's practise slowing down together. The girl smiled. At her old club, the coach only said: Try harder. She told her mother that this new feedback was the first that made her want to train.

prompt.es: Lee la situación y elige la versión mejorada del comentario «Good job».

choices.text: Good job: I noticed that you answered every question calmly; next time, add an example.
Good job, you are clearly the best speaker in the whole group, and everyone knows it.
Good job, but your answers were terrible in the middle.

feedback.es: La versión mejorada cita un hecho y propone un paso; las otras son elogio vago o ataque.

origin.text: A manager wants to improve the comment Good job, which she wrote after a colleague's interview. She wants it to say what went well and what to try next, but still be respectful.

feedback.es: I suggest you + verbo base formula una recomendación concreta sin ser una orden.

origin.text: The manager does not give an order. She says, in a calm and respectful voice: I ___ you add one example to your next talk.

prompt.es: ¿Qué frase reconoce la emoción del equipo antes de empezar a criticar?

We lost because you did not follow the plan that we agreed.
It was only a game, so nobody should feel disappointed about it today.

prompt.es: Escucha la charla y elige cómo abre la entrenadora su intervención.

choices.text: By pointing out the mistake that cost the match.
By recognising how the players feel about the loss.
By praising the captain for the goals that she scored.

feedback.es: Empieza con la emoción («the defeat hurts»); la crítica llega después con However.

origin.audio: The final whistle went, and the players sat in silence. The coach sat in front of them. I know the defeat hurts, she said, and you have every right to feel disappointed. Then she looked at the captain. Despite the defeat, I'm proud of how you defended in the second half. However, we lost the ball too often in the middle, and that is fixable. She paused. What will it take for us to bounce back next Saturday? Nobody answered, but a few players were already nodding.

prompt.es: Con la misma charla, elige qué sugiere que algunos jugadores asientan.

choices.text: They agree that the coach was unfair to the captain in the second half.
They believe that the defeat was nobody's fault.
They accept the challenge and start thinking about the next match.

feedback.es: Nadie responde, pero asentir indica que la pregunta les hace pensar en cómo recuperarse.

origin.text: Tu equipo perdió 3-2. Escribe una frase que reconozca un esfuerzo concreto (la velocidad en el ataque) y continúe con however y una crítica concreta (dejaron demasiado espacio atrás).

prompt.es: Escribe la charla del entrenador tras la derrota.

answer.text:
Team, sit down for a moment. I know this defeat hurts, and it is fine to feel disappointed. I feel the same.
First, I want to say what I saw. Despite the defeat, I'm proud of how you defended in the second half. Mia, your two tackles saved us three times, and Tom, you never stopped talking to the team. You deserve credit for that.
However, we lost the ball too often in the middle of the pitch, and that gave them the chance to score. It is only one thing, and it is fixable. One match does not decide our season.
So let me ask you: what would it take for us to keep the ball longer next Saturday? What could we try in training on Thursday? I would like to hear two ideas from each of you.
Go home, rest, and come back ready to learn. I believe in this team.
accepted:
Team, sit down for a moment. I know this defeat hurts, and it is fine to feel disappointed. I feel the same.
First, I want to say what I saw. Despite the defeat, I'm proud of how you defended in the second half. Mia, your two tackles saved us three times, and Tom, you never stopped talking to the team. You deserve credit for that.
However, we lost the ball too often in the middle of the pitch, and that gave them the chance to score. It is only one thing, and it is fixable. One match does not decide our season.
So let me ask you: what would it take for us to keep the ball longer next Saturday? What could we try in training on Thursday? I would like to hear two ideas from each of you.
Go home, rest, and come back ready to learn. I believe in this team.

Everyone, come here. I know how painful this defeat is, and I understand you are disappointed. I am too.
I want to start with what worked. I'm proud of how you supported each other during the last twenty minutes. Leo, your effort in defence was excellent, and Sara, you encouraged everybody until the final whistle.
However, we waited too long before we shot, and they blocked our chances easily. That is one concrete thing to improve, and it is not a disaster.
Now, what would help us to use the whole field next week? What is stopping us from looking for the right side? What could we try first on Tuesday? Think about it tonight, and tell me tomorrow.
It was a tough day, but you deserve to be proud of your effort. We will bounce back, and I will be with you on Saturday.

feedback.es: Una buena charla reconoce la emoción y dos esfuerzos concretos, hace una crítica específica con however y cierra con una pregunta de coaching.

origin.text: Tu equipo perdió 2–1 la final del barrio. Escribe la charla del entrenador (unas 200–250 palabras): reconoce la emoción y dos esfuerzos concretos (la defensa y el ánimo), señala una crítica concreta (por ejemplo, balones perdidos en el medio) y cierra con un plan formulado como pregunta de coaching.

prompt.es: Escucha el correo de la capitana y elige qué actitud muestra hacia la charla.

She thinks the talk should have avoided any criticism.

feedback.es: La capitana agradece la charla pero pide más detalle sobre los errores: le gusta y exige concreción.

origin.audio: After the heavy defeat, the captain wrote an email to the coach. She said the talk had helped, but added that one sentence had stayed in her mind: It is only a setback. She explained that it had stopped her from blaming herself. In the same email she asked for more detail about the mistakes, because praise alone, she wrote, would not help the team improve.

prompt.es: Con el mismo correo, elige por qué menciona la frase «It is only a setback».

choices.text: Because it made her forget about the defeat entirely and stay calm.
Because it helped her stop blaming herself for the result.
Because it convinced her that nothing needed to change.

feedback.es: La frase la ayudó a dejar de culparse, pero ella sigue pidiendo detalles para mejorar: no olvidó la derrota.

The players talked about it all evening.

prompt.es: Lee la queja del jugador y elige la respuesta que reconoce, critica y propone un paso.

origin.audio: On Saturday morning, the coordinator of a community garden spoke to the volunteers to tell them about a change. Starting next month, she said, there will be two shifts instead of one, because more families are coming and we need more time to welcome them. She explained that each volunteer would choose a shift by Friday, and that a guide and a buddy would support anyone who felt unsure. One volunteer asked whether the early shift was required. The coordinator smiled and asked: What would make it easier for you to come in the morning?

prompt.es: Con el mismo anuncio, elige con qué propósito pregunta la coordinadora al voluntario.

choices.text: To involve the volunteer in finding a solution.
To check that he understands the new rules.
To persuade him to cancel his other plans.

feedback.es: La pregunta de coaching invita al voluntario a buscar una solución con ella, en lugar de imponerle una.

origin.text: Thank you all for coming this morning. I want to ___ a change in our Saturday schedule, and I want to explain why.

prompt.es: Escribe el anuncio del cambio a los voluntarios.

answer.text:
Hi everyone,
Thank you for coming. I want to announce a change in our Saturday schedule. The reason is simple: more families are coming to the garden, and we need more time to help them.
Here is the plan. First, we will have two shifts instead of one: nine to twelve, and twelve to three. Second, each volunteer will choose a shift by Friday. Third, we will review the plan in a month.
We will support you with a clear guide and a buddy for your first week. Nobody will work alone.
Tom, I understand your concern about the early start. It sounds like you feel stressed because you study at night. What would make the afternoon shift easier for you?
Ana, I hear that you are worried about the new register. What would help you feel more confident? I can practise it with you on Thursday.
I know change is tough, but I am proud of what this team does every week. Thank you for your effort, and please tell me what you think.

Dear volunteers,
I want to announce a change for Saturdays. The reason is that many more families are coming to the garden, and our morning is now too short.
This is the plan. We will work in two shifts, one in the morning and one in the afternoon. Each of you can choose the shift that suits you best. We will review the schedule after four weeks, and then we will decide together if we keep it.
Of course, we will support you. You will receive a short guide, and an experienced volunteer will help you during the first week.
Tom, I understand your concern. You study at night, so the early start is hard. What would make the afternoon shift possible for you?
Ana, it sounds like you feel worried about the new register. What could we try so that you feel more confident? I am happy to practise it with you.
Change is never easy, but your effort makes a real difference. Thank you for your patience and your ideas.

origin.text: Eres coordinador de un huerto comunitario. Los sábados habrá dos turnos (9–12 y 12–15) porque vienen más familias. prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué actitud adopta la coordinadora ante la queja de la voluntaria.

origin.audio: After the announcement, one volunteer stayed behind. I am not against the change, she told the coordinator, but nobody asked us before deciding. The coordinator did not defend the decision. She said: It sounds like you feel left out of the process, and you need to be heard earlier. That is fair. What would make it easier to give you a voice next time? The volunteer relaxed and said she would join the new shift.

prompt.es: Con la misma escena, elige qué se deduce del final de la conversación.

choices.text: She had only now realised that the change was really necessary.
She joined the new shift only because she had no choice.
Her concern was more about being heard than about the shift itself.

feedback.es: La voluntaria se relaja al sentirse escuchada y acepta el turno: su queja era sobre el proceso, no sobre el horario.

origin.audio: Who will speak for a child who cannot vote? This year, three children almost had an accident at our school gate. The council calls it a minor delay; I call it a matter of life. And I will say this slowly, because it matters: a crossing is not a luxury. It is a need.

prompt.es: Escribe tu discurso por el paso de peatones y responde a dos objeciones.

answer.text: Who will speak for a child who cannot vote? This year, three children almost had an accident at our school gate. What we need is a safe crossing. Our survey is clear: 82% of families support it. Some of you may say it will cost too much. I understand your concern, but one accident would cost far more. Others say it will cause a delay to the traffic. That is a fair point; however, two minutes of delay is nothing next to a child's safety. Never before have so many parents asked for something so simple. It is our children who cross that road every morning, and it is we who must protect them. Let me be clear: a crossing is not a luxury, it is a need. I do not ask you for a favour; I ask you for what every child in this town deserves, and I ask you to stand with me tonight. So please sign the petition before Friday, because our children cannot wait.

origin.text: Datos: paso de peatones seguro frente a la escuela. Este año, tres niños casi fueron atropellados. Una encuesta halló que el 82 % de las familias lo apoya. Objeciones: «cuesta demasiado» y «retrasará el tráfico». Petición final: firmar la petición antes del viernes. Incluye gancho, dato, dos recursos de énfasis, respuesta a las dos objeciones y una petición final.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige por qué la oradora empieza respondiendo con «I hear that concern».

choices.text: To avoid the question by changing the subject to the survey.
To admit that the objection is right and stop asking for signatures.

origin.audio: A question came from the back of the hall: is a crossing not a waste of public money? The speaker took a breath and paused. Nobody moved, and she did not raise her voice once. I hear that concern, she said, and I will not pretend that money is no object. But the survey is clear: eighty-two per cent of parents feel afraid at the gate, and three children were almost hurt there this year. So please sign before Friday.

Leo was not angry, though: he said the surprise had already cost an arm and a leg, and that he did not want to lose a friend over it as well.

I will keep my messages simple this week, and please tell me whenever something is not clear. See you there.

answer.text: Hi team, the book fair starts on Monday, so we need to hit the ground running. In other words, we start work early and every person needs to know their task. Let's touch base on Friday for a short meeting to check our progress. I must also be honest: the delay with the posters is only the tip of the iceberg, because we still need more volunteers. In plain words, we have more problems than we thought, so please tell me if you can help. I do not want to use many idioms, so I will keep the rest simple. The plan is clear: posters on Tuesday, volunteers by Wednesday, and a last meeting on Friday. If any of you is not sure about a task, write to me tonight, and I will explain it in simple words. We are a small team, but I am sure that, working together, we can make this book fair a real success. Thank you for your work, and see you on Monday at eight!

Hello everyone, our book fair begins on Monday, so we have to hit the ground running. In other words, we start quickly and we all know our tasks. Let's touch base on Friday for a brief meeting. The delay with the posters is the tip of the iceberg, because we also need more volunteers. In plain words, there are more problems than we expected, so please tell me how you can help. I do not want to use many idioms, so I will keep the rest simple. The plan is clear: posters on Tuesday, volunteers by Wednesday, and a final meeting on Friday. Every person should know their task before Monday morning, and if something is not clear, please write to me tonight and I will explain it in simple words. We are a small team, but together we can make this fair a great success. Thanks a lot for your help!

prompt.es: Responde al mensaje de Sol: explica los dos modismos en inglés sencillo.

answer.text: Hi Sol, sorry about that. Those are idioms, and they do not mean what the words say. “Back to square one” means that we have to start again from the beginning. We made a plan, but it did not work, so we are at the start again. “Hit the nail on the head” means to say exactly the right thing. When Leo said the price was too high, he hit the nail on the head, because that was exactly the problem. In other words, the first idiom is about starting again and the second is about being exactly right. Let me put it simply: nobody is playing a game, and nobody is using a hammer. Does that make sense? If not, I can rephrase it or spell it out step by step. I will also write without idioms next time, so please tell me if any other phrase is unclear. I do not want anything to get lost in translation. Thank you for asking, and thanks for your patience!
accepted: Hi Sol, sorry about that. Those are idioms, and they do not mean what the words say. “Back to square one” means that we have to start again from the beginning. Hello Sol, sorry, I used idioms. “Back to square one” means we must start again from the beginning, because our first plan did not work. “Hit the nail on the head” means to say exactly the right thing. Leo said the price was too high, and he was exactly right. In other words, the first idiom means we start again and the second means someone is correct. Is that clear? I can also spell it out step by step if you like, and next time I will use simple words, so please tell me if something is unclear. I do not want anything to get lost in translation, and I never want to talk down to you. Thanks for asking, and thank you for being so patient with our team. Do not hesitate to write to me again if another phrase is unclear to you.

origin.audio: The regional manager's report was blunt. Since the decision to change carrier, the company's growth has slowed for two quarters, partly because the failure of the old carrier to meet its deadlines had already cost us several clients. The manager added that the refusal of the old carrier to discuss compensation had finally made the change unavoidable, and that it should have been made years ago.

origin.text: Three years ago the council decided to build a new library in our neighbourhood, and everybody was pleased. However, the builders were late because there were not enough skilled workers in the region, so the work fell behind schedule. As a result, the library opened a full year late, and many families were angry and sent letters of complaint to the council. Some of them even gathered outside the building every Saturday morning to ask when it would open. While they waited, the price of materials rose sharply, because the suppliers could not deliver on time, and the council had to pay the workers for extra months. The mayor visited the site twice, and each time the builders promised that the next month would be better. In the wake of these problems, the newspaper asked why nobody had planned for the risk, and the council promised that it would investigate the matter. Finally, the library opened in September, and many of those families stayed for hours in the new rooms. The council had spent much more money than it had planned, but the result was good: every week more than a thousand people visit, and the children read much more than before. Looking back, the director says that the delay taught the council to plan more carefully, and that the families who complained deserve thanks, because their letters made the council act.

answer.text: The fast expansion of community gardens in European cities has led to a marked reduction in stress and in food costs for many families, according to a growing body of evidence. origin.text: Community gardens are spreading fast through European cities. In many capitals, empty corners that used to be ignored by everybody are now full of vegetables and flowers. In the last ten years, thousands of neighbours have started to grow vegetables together on small plots of public land, and a growing body of evidence suggests that the benefits go well beyond fresh food. Researchers who followed four hundred gardeners for two years report a marked reduction in stress, and many families say that they now spend less money on food. One gardener, a retired teacher, says that she knows more neighbours now than she did in thirty years in the same street. Participation has also brought people together: in several districts, neighbours who had never spoken now share tools, seeds and advice. Local newspapers have run many stories about the gardens, and several mayors have visited them. However, the expansion has a clear limit. Vacant land is scarce, and councils disagree about the allocation of the plots. In some districts a neighbour may wait three years for a plot. Some want to give them first to schools, others to older residents, and a few argue that the places should go to whoever has waited longest. One researcher warns that the lack of a fair system could turn a popular project into a source of anger. A key finding of the study is that gardens work well when residents help to make the rules. The next step, she says, is a transparent system that every neighbour can understand and trust.

answer.text: Dear Tom, I think there was a misunderstanding at the dinner on Friday, and I would like to clear the air. I did not intend to offend you, and I am very sorry that my insistence on paying may have come across as rude. In my country it is a custom for the person who invites to pay for everybody, and refusing your offer was my way of showing respect, not of ignoring you. I can see now that it may have given the wrong impression, since in Scotland friends usually share the bill. I apologise for not explaining this at the time, and I hope you will give me the benefit of the doubt. Let me clarify something else: I enjoyed the evening very much, and I appreciate your honesty when you told me how you felt. Perhaps we could meet halfway next time: I will choose the restaurant, and you will pay for the dessert. Would you like to have lunch on Saturday? I promise to ask before I reach for the bill. Kind regards, Mia

Hello Tom, I am sorry about the confusion at the dinner. I think we had a misunderstanding, and I never meant to hurt you. Where I come from, the person who invites usually pays for everybody, so when I refused your offer I wanted to show respect, but I see that it may have given the wrong impression and come across as rude to you. I apologise for not explaining that at the moment. Let me clarify: I had a lovely evening, and I want to keep our friendship. I appreciate that you told me how you felt, and I hope you can give me the benefit of the doubt. Perhaps we could go out again on Saturday, and this time we could split the bill so that nobody feels uncomfortable. Would you like that? Thank you for listening.

answer.text: I still remember the night I missed the last train. I was a student, and I had spent the whole evening at a friend's birthday party in the next town. When I reached the station, the platform was empty and the clock showed midnight. My phone had no battery, and the nearest taxi was far away. I sat on a cold bench and tried to stay calm. It was not the dark that frightened me; it was the silence. Never had I heard a city so quiet. Then, behind me, I heard footsteps. They were slow, and they were coming closer. I held my bag tightly and did not look back. 'Are you waiting for the last train?' a voice asked. I looked up, and my heart stopped. The man in front of me was wearing a long grey coat, and he looked strangely familiar. He turned out to be Mr Duarte, my new science teacher, who lived two streets away. He smiled, offered me a lift and even gave me his phone charger. All the way home I kept thinking about how afraid I had been of a person who only wanted to help. Looking back, I realise that the real problem was not the empty station. It was my habit of expecting the worst and of staying silent when I needed help. Since that night, I ask for help earlier, and I listen for the kind voice before I imagine the dangerous one.

The night I missed the last train began like any other. I was at a party in the next town, and I left too late. On the platform, the clock showed midnight and nobody was there. I sat down and waited, because my phone had no battery. What frightened me most was the silence. Then I heard footsteps behind me, slow and close. I did not dare to look. The lights were weak, and the wind moved some old paper along the ground. A voice said, 'Are you waiting for the last train?' I looked up, and there was my new science teacher, Mr Duarte, in a long grey coat. It turned out that he lived nearby, and he offered me a lift home. In the car we hardly spoke, but it was warm, and the radio played softly. I felt almost ashamed. I had been afraid of a man who only wanted to help. Looking back, I learned that I often expect the worst when I am alone. Never again will I stay silent when I need help.

prompt.es: Escribe una anécdota de unas 150 palabras con escena, giro y desenlace.

answer.text: It was a grey afternoon, and the rain was tapping on the windows of the library. I was about to return a book when I noticed a small note between the pages. Suddenly, my curiosity woke up. It was a phone number, and below it someone had written: “Call me if you find this.” I was going to throw the note away, but then I remembered how quiet the library could feel on a wet day, so I phoned. A woman answered at once. “Finally,” she said, laughing. “I left it there three years ago, as a joke.” We talked for an hour. Little did I know that she would become my business partner, and that we would open a small shop together. To my relief, the shop was an immediate success, and the note is still on the wall.

It was a rainy evening, and the wind was blowing hard outside the station. A few people were waiting quietly in the dark. I was about to get on the last bus when it dawned on me that my wallet was not in my bag. My heart was beating very fast. I was going to ask the driver for help, but a young woman handed me a ticket. “Don't worry,” she said. “Buy me a coffee one day.” I thanked her and sat by the window. Little did I know that I would meet her again. Two weeks later, she came into my new office, and she would become my best friend for the rest of my life, and my business partner too.

feedback.es: Una buena anécdota abre con una escena en pasado continuo, la rompe con un hecho, usa was about to / was going to y anticipa el final con would (Little did I know…).

origin.text: Situación: una tarde de lluvia en la biblioteca de tu barrio. Ibas a devolver un libro cuando viste una nota con un número de teléfono entre las páginas. Ibas a tirarla, pero llamaste. origin.audio: It was a wet Sunday, and the train to Bristol was packed. I was sitting by the window, tapping my foot on the floor, when a man across from me dropped his wallet. I was about to call out when I noticed a card sticking out of it: “If lost, please return to Mr Hall.” I handed it back and thought nothing more of it. Little did I know that Mr Hall owned the company where I had applied for a job. As luck would have it, he remembered my face on the day of the interview, and within a month I had signed my contract.

prompt.es: Cuenta la anécdota (unas 170 palabras) y responde a las dos preguntas del público.

answer.text:
Every summer, the whole family used to meet at my grandmother's house. The kitchen smelled of coffee, and the relatives were all talking at once. My aunt Mia would always tell the same story about the day she lost her umbrella at the station. That year, she was about to start it again when a stranger walked into the garden, holding an old umbrella. Nobody recognised him. Silence. Then my aunt stood up and put her hand to her face. “It's mine,” she whispered. He had been looking for her for thirty years, and he had kept the umbrella in his house all that time. Little did we know that he would stay for dinner, and that he would become part of the family.
Did you recognise him? No, I didn't. I thought he was a neighbour.
What did your aunt say? Fair enough, she said. Tonight, for once, we will hear a new story.
accepted:
Every summer, the whole family used to meet at my grandmother's house. The kitchen smelled of coffee, and the relatives were all talking at once. My aunt Mia would always tell the same story about the day she lost her umbrella at the station. That year, she was about to start it again when a stranger walked into the garden, holding an old umbrella. Nobody recognised him. Silence. Then my aunt stood up and put her hand to her face. “It's mine,” she whispered. He had been looking for her for thirty years, and he had kept the umbrella in his house all that time. Little did we know that he would stay for dinner, and that he would become part of the family.
Did you recognise him? No, I didn't. I thought he was a neighbour.
What did your aunt say? Fair enough, she said. Tonight, for once, we will hear a new story.

When I was a child, we would all meet at my grandmother's house on Sundays. The kitchen smelled of bread, and the relatives were laughing in the garden. My aunt Mia used to tell the same story about the day she lost her umbrella at the station. One Sunday, she was about to begin when a tall man walked into the garden with an umbrella in his hand. Nobody knew him. Silence. Then my aunt smiled and opened her arms. “That's my umbrella,” she said. He had been searching for her for thirty years, and he had never given up. Little did I know that he would become my uncle's best friend.
Did you recognise him? No, I didn't. I thought he was a friend of my uncle.
What did your aunt say? Honestly, she said nothing. She just hugged him.

feedback.es: Una buena versión abre con hábito o escena, rompe con un hecho o was about to, da el giro con had been o Little did we know y responde a las dos preguntas del público (reconocerlo y qué dijo tu tía) con respuestas cortas.

origin.text: Situación: reunión familiar en casa de tu abuela. Cada verano tu tía Mia contaba la historia del día que perdió su paraguas en la estación. Un año, iba a empezar cuando un desconocido entró en el jardín con un paraguas viejo: era el hombre que lo había encontrado hacía treinta años y llevaba todo ese tiempo buscándola. Cuenta la anécdota (unas 170 palabras) con: un hábito o escena del pasado (used to / would), un hecho con was about to, un giro con had been o Little did we know y un final corto. feedback.es: Nadie lo ayudó porque querían oírlo encontrar el final: lo que valoran es la costumbre de escucharlo, no los detalles de la historia.

origin.audio: Every year, at the family reunion, my uncle Carlos would tell the same story about the night he met my aunt. He would embellish it a little more each time, until the rain became a storm and the walk became a mountain climb. The distant relatives would smile politely, and my cousins would count the new details. Yet nobody ever stopped him. When he reached the punchline, the whole table burst out laughing, even those who could have told it word for word. Last year he forgot the ending. Nobody helped him. For once, we all just wanted to hear him find it.

prompt.es: Completa: «Adorna sus historias: cada vez que las cuenta, el pez crece.»

feedback.es: Embellish es la palabra precisa para adornar un relato; exaggerate y embroider también son posibles, pero embellish subraya el adorno más que la exageración.

origin.text: Every time he tells it, the fish gets bigger. He likes to ___ his stories a little, and nobody minds.

feedback.es: La pausa y «Let's say I got carried away» revelan que adorna la respuesta para divertir; la risa posterior confirma que el público entiende el juego.

prompt.es: ¿Cuál es la postura del autor sobre las historias familiares?

choices.text: That they should be checked against the real facts.
That they reveal more about the family than the event, which is a problem.
That they need not be strictly accurate to be worth telling.
That a good punchline matters more than any other detail.

feedback.es: «Yet that, surely, is the point» defiende que la inexactitud es lo que da sentido a estas historias: no buscan informar, sino reflejar a la familia, y el autor no lo lamenta.

origin.text: Family stories are rarely accurate. Every retelling embellishes them, drops the awkward details and improves the punchline, until the tale says more about the family than about the event. Yet that, surely, is the point: nobody at a reunion wants a report; they want to hear themselves described, a little taller and a little funnier than they were.

origin.audio: Our flight was delayed for nine hours, the airline lost my suitcase, and the hotel had given our room to somebody else. When the receptionist asked my brother how the journey had been, he said, with a perfectly straight face, that it had been “a bit of a mixed start”.

feedback.es: «Only three hours» y «a great success» suenan a elogio, pero describen un atasco: la queja se esconde tras un agradecimiento exagerado.

origin.text: Thank you for warning us about the traffic. We only spent three hours in the queue, and I am sure the extra time in the car was good for our conversation. The children are still speaking to us, so I suppose the day was a great success.

prompt.es: Escucha el relato: ¿qué da a entender la vecina con su comentario sobre el viaje?

choices.text: That she regrets having planned a journey for that week.
That the snow has been only a minor nuisance for the village.
That the situation is serious, but she prefers to treat it lightly.
That she is annoyed with the reporter for arriving so late.

feedback.es: Nueve días aislados hacen de «not exactly the best week» un understatement: la vecina quita importancia a algo grave con humor.

origin.audio: Last winter my village was cut off by snow for nine days. The power failed, the only shop ran out of bread, and the road disappeared under a metre of white. On the third day a reporter arrived on foot and asked my neighbour how everyone was feeling. She sighed, looked at the drifts and said that it had not exactly been the best week for travelling. The reporter wrote it down as if it were a serious remark. The rest of us laughed for an hour, because my neighbour had not left her kitchen since Sunday and had baked forty loaves to feed the street.

feedback.es: Elogia justo lo que no debería haberse hecho (omitir cifras) y cierra con «transparency»: la crítica va envuelta en un elogio irónico.

origin.text: Thanks for your report. I read it on the train and was surprised by how brave you were to leave out every figure that might have upset the client. It is, of course, the kind of omission that makes my job very simple. I shall be sure to tell the board how well you understand our commitment to transparency.

prompt.es: ¿Cuál es la postura del autor del blog sobre el humor británico?

choices.text: It is indirect rather than unfriendly, and must be interpreted.
It is cold, but visitors are too quick to take offence.
It is best avoided by anyone who cannot read faces.
It is always ironic, so compliments are never sincere.

feedback.es: El autor rechaza que sea «cold»: lo llama «careful» y propone comprobar cada elogio contra los hechos, no descartarlos todos.

origin.text: People tell me that British humour is cold. I would say it is merely careful: we rarely announce our feelings, so a polite “that was interesting” after a terrible dinner can mean almost anything. The key is to watch the face, weigh the situation and never take a compliment at face value until you have checked it against the facts.

origin.audio: A friend of mine teaches English, and his favourite joke is about a student who ate his homework. The teacher asked why, and the boy answered that the exercise had been a piece of cake. The class groaned, but the teacher admitted that the joke was not bad.

prompt.es: Lee la anécdota: ¿por qué no funcionó el chiste con la prima?

She disliked jokes about bicycles and said so.
She heard the wrong word and missed the homophone.
She understood both senses but thought them silly.

feedback.es: La prima entendió «two» como un número de ruedas: no percibió el homófono too, y por eso el remate se quedó sin efecto.

origin.text: When my cousin heard the joke about the bicycle that could not stand up because it was two tired, she asked why two wheels were a problem. I explained that the word was really too, and that the bicycle was also tired. She nodded politely, but the pun had already lost its effect.

prompt.es: Ordena: «La última palabra del chiste lleva los dos sentidos.»

answer.text: The last word of the pun carries both meanings

feedback.es: El sujeto es the last word of the pun; carries both meanings describe su función en el remate.

prompt.es: Escucha al humorista: ¿cómo interpreta el quejido del público?

choices.text: As a mild complaint that audiences make against humour the critics call the lowest form.
As a signal that the preparation took too long for the punchline to surprise anyone.
As an honest reaction that he has learned to accept, although it still hurts a little.
As proof that the listener understood the joke and enjoyed it in spite of himself.

feedback.es: Para el humorista el quejido no es un insulto sino «the highest compliment»: demuestra que el oyente entendió el remate a su pesar.

origin.audio: On the radio last week, a performer explained why he loves puns, even bad ones. A good pun, he said, is a small piece of engineering: the preparation builds one meaning, the punchline switches to another, and the audience has half a second to feel proud. Then comes the groan. He claimed that the groan is not an offence but the highest compliment, because it shows that the listener has understood and cannot forgive himself for enjoying it. Critics say that puns are the lowest form of humour. He smiled and said that they are, but that is exactly why people remember them.

prompt.es: Lee la carta al periódico: ¿qué critica en realidad quien la escribe?

choices.text: The habit of using wordplay instead of informing readers.
The use of any wordplay in a serious newspaper.
The lack of humour in modern headlines.
The decision to give bank news the front page.

feedback.es: El autor acepta el wordplay, pero rechaza que sustituya a la información: su objeción es al hábito, no a los juegos de palabras en sí.

origin.text: Your headline about the bank thief making a run for it might have made me smile if I had not read the same kind of pun three times this month. Headline writers seem to think that any word with two meanings deserves the front page. I do not object to wordplay; I object to wordplay that takes the place of information.

prompt.es: Completa: «El chiste depende de la última palabra.»

feedback.es: Hinges on expresa que todo el efecto depende de un único elemento: aquí, la palabra clave del remate.

origin.text: Nothing in the preparation is funny by itself. The whole joke ___ on the last word, which means one thing in the story and another in the punchline.

prompt.es: ¿Con qué propósito defiende los juegos de palabras quien escribe?

choices.text: To persuade pupils to write more jokes of their own.
To show that analysing puns trains useful language skills.
To admit that puns are silly but not dangerous.
To argue that language exercises are useless.

feedback.es: Para ella analizar un pun es «a demanding exercise» que enseña más lengua que marcar casillas: defiende su valor formativo.

origin.text: Some pupils complain that puns are silly. I would argue the opposite: to build a pun, you must hold two meanings in your head at once, and that is a demanding exercise. A pupil who can explain why a joke works has understood more language than one who simply fills in a worksheet.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Nadie se rió, pero el juego de palabras hizo que todos gimieran.»

answer.text: Nobody laughed, but the pun made everyone groan

feedback.es: Make + objeto + verbo base (made everyone groan) expresa que el chiste provoca la reacción.

prompt.es: Escucha el mensaje de voz: ¿qué le sugiere Leo a Ana?

choices.text: To cut the wordplay from the title because readers may find it too hard.
To explain the pun in a short note printed below the title.
To move the wordplay to the ending so it can surprise readers.
To choose a longer title that contains even more wordplay.

feedback.es: Leo aprecia el pun, pero cree que el título adelanta el final: propone reservarlo para la última línea, donde sorprende.

origin.audio: Hi Ana, it is Leo. I read your draft for the school newspaper. The pun in your title is good, but I think it gives away the ending. Perhaps you could keep the wordplay for the last line, where the punchline can really surprise people.

prompt.es: Lee la escena: ¿qué pista delata que Carlos no es sincero?

choices.text: The schedule was new, so he is confused.
His flat voice and sigh contradict his words.
His words are positive, so they are sincere.

feedback.es: Carlos dice que todo está claro, pero el suspiro y la voz plana van en sentido contrario: el tono delata el sarcasmo.

hint.es: Mira qué hacen su voz y su cuerpo mientras habla.

origin.text: After Sara had explained the new schedule for the third time, Carlos sighed, looked at the ceiling and said in a flat voice, “Oh, that is so clear now.”

prompt.es: Completa: «Fue un viaje tan largo que todos nos dormimos.»

feedback.es: Con un nombre (journey) detrás del adjetivo se usa such a; so solo acompañaría a un adjetivo suelto.

hint.es: Después del espacio vienen a + adjetivo + nombre.

origin.text: The train was delayed twice, and then it stopped for an hour in an empty field. It was ___ a long journey that we all fell asleep.

feedback.es: Las cuatro son pistas de sarcasmo: dos de tono, una de contexto y una de contenido.

prompt.es: Escucha la escena: ¿qué quiere decir Mia con «you are so reliable»?

choices.text: That Leo has done well and deserves thanks.
That Leo is reliable, although he forgot one thing.
That Leo is not reliable, and she is annoyed.

feedback.es: El suspiro y las manos vacías contradicen el elogio: Mia usa «reliable» con sarcasmo para reprochar el olvido.

origin.audio: Leo had promised to bring the tickets for the concert, but he arrived at the station with empty hands. Mia looked at him, gave a long sigh and said, “Well, you are so reliable.” Everybody laughed except Leo, who stared at the floor.

prompt.es: Lee el fragmento: ¿qué hace sarcástico el segundo comentario de Sara?

choices.text: She repeats the word plan in both remarks.
She speaks while she is busy with her phone.
She uses a longer sentence than in her first remark.
The praise comes just after she finds the Sunday meetings.

feedback.es: El contexto decide: felicita a Carlos justo cuando descubre reuniones en domingo, así que el elogio es una crítica disfrazada.

origin.text: Carlos handed Sara the new schedule. “It is such a lovely plan,” said Sara, without looking up from her phone. Then she put the phone down, turned the page, found the same meetings on Sunday, and added, “Really, you have thought of everything.”

prompt.es: Ordena: «Fue una reunión tan larga que todos suspiraron.»

answer.text: It was such a long meeting that everybody sighed

feedback.es: Such a + adjetivo + nombre va seguido de that + resultado: la estructura intensifica y explica la consecuencia.

prompt.es: Escucha el relato: ¿cómo responde la jefa al comentario de Carlos?

choices.text: She has understood the sarcasm and answers it with a polite challenge.
She takes his remark as a genuine compliment and rewards him with a new task.
She feels hurt by his comment and brings the meeting to an end at once.
She accepts that the rota needs more work and thanks him for his honesty.

feedback.es: Sonríe y le pide que organice el siguiente: es un desafío cortés que muestra que captó el sarcasmo, y Carlos lo entiende así.

origin.audio: Our manager presented the new weekend rota for the third time, and each time it had changed. When she finished, my colleague Carlos put his hand up and said, in a perfectly flat voice, that he had rarely seen such a well organised plan. Nobody spoke. The manager smiled, thanked him warmly and asked whether he would like to help organise the next one. Carlos went pale and said that, on reflection, the plan was not so bad. Afterwards Sara whispered that she respected his courage, because sarcasm is always a risk when the listener is also the boss.

prompt.es: ¿Cuál es la postura de quien escribe sobre el sarcasmo con su hijo adolescente?

choices.text: It is dangerous, so she should never use it with young people.
It is acceptable when the son can answer back in the same way.
It is better than a lecture in every family conversation she has.
It is a habit that she has copied from her own sixteen-year-old son.

feedback.es: No lo rechaza ni lo defiende sin más: lo acepta mientras el hijo pueda responder igual, porque solo duele cuando no hay réplica.

origin.text: I am told that I should not use sarcasm with my sixteen-year-old son. Perhaps so. But when he says that cleaning his room is a lovely chance, he is hardly sincere himself, and I find a dry reply more honest than a lecture. Sarcasm only hurts when the listener has no chance to answer in kind.

prompt.es: Completa: «Fue un cumplido envenenado, cortés por fuera e hiriente por dentro.»

feedback.es: Backhanded compliment es la colocación para un elogio que contiene una crítica: amable en apariencia, hiriente en el fondo.

origin.text: When Sara won the prize, her opponent said, “Congratulations, you must be surprised that the judges chose you.” It was a ___ compliment, polite on the surface and rude inside.
