prompt.es: ¿Qué da a entender la abuela con su comentario sobre el traje?

choices.text: That she respects his courage in choosing the colour.
That he will be easy to find if he gets lost.
That the suit is too loud, though she avoids saying so.
That she would prefer him to buy a different suit.

feedback.es: La abuela nunca critica de frente: «nobody will lose you» es un cumplido con doble filo, y el resto de la familia capta el tono.

origin.text: My grandmother never says anything rude. When my cousin arrived in a bright orange suit, she looked him up and down and said, “Well, nobody will lose you in a crowd.” He took it as a compliment. The rest of the family, who know her tone, did not.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Nadie le creyó, porque su voz plana lo delató.»

answer.text: Nobody believed him because his flat voice gave the game away

feedback.es: Give the game away lleva el objeto en medio: gave the game away, con la causa introducida por because.

prompt.es: Escucha la anécdota: ¿por qué entiende el camarero la queja al instante?

choices.text: Because the uncle had complained about the same soup several times before.
Because the uncle asked him openly to change the soup.
Because the waiter had already noticed that the soup was cold.
Because what the uncle said clashed with what was plainly on the table.

feedback.es: Elogiar una «warm welcome» ante un plato frío es un contraste evidente: el camarero capta la queja sin que se formule.

origin.audio: When the waiter asked how the soup was, my uncle looked at the cold bowl, sighed and said that it was such a warm welcome. The waiter understood at once and offered to heat it up, because the contrast between the words and the bowl was painfully clear.

prompt.es: Lee el mensaje de Tom: ¿cuál es la hipérbole?

choices.text: honestly, it was kind of a disaster
but I am only joking about the whole thing
so long that I could have written a novel

feedback.es: La hipérbole es el resultado absurdo con so… that; kind of y only joking son los suavizadores que rebajan el tono.

hint.es: Busca la parte que nadie podría creer al pie de la letra.

origin.text: Tom sent his friend a message after the concert: “The queue was so long that I could have written a novel. Honestly, it was kind of a disaster, but I am only joking.”

prompt.es: Completa: «Ni mi hermano ni mi hermana probaron un trozo.»

feedback.es: Neither se completa siempre con nor, nunca con or: los dos elementos quedan descartados.

hint.es: Es la pareja negativa de neither.

origin.text: The pizza was so small that I could have eaten it in one bite, and neither my brother ___ my sister got a single slice.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Fue una cola tan larga que aprendí italiano.»

answer.text: It was such a long queue that I learned Italian

feedback.es: Such a + adjetivo + nombre va seguido de that + resultado absurdo: la hipérbole queda completa.

hint.es: Such a va antes del adjetivo y del nombre; that introduce el resultado.

prompt.es: Escucha el mensaje: ¿qué hace la hablante con «the driver is on holiday»?

choices.text: She exaggerates to be funny and then softens the remark.
She reports a rumour that she has heard from other passengers.
She makes a serious accusation and then regrets it at once.

feedback.es: Nadie cree que el conductor esté de vacaciones: es una hipérbole cómica que «only joking» suaviza inmediatamente.

origin.audio: I have been standing at this bus stop for so long that the birds know me by name. The timetable promises a bus every ten minutes, but I am almost certain that the driver is on holiday. Only joking, of course. I am sure that he will arrive soon, and I will forgive him at once.

prompt.es: Lee la respuesta a Tom: ¿por qué podría resultar ofensiva?

choices.text: It mocks Tom's own effort, and the softener comes too late.
It exaggerates so much that nobody could possibly believe a single word.
It contains no softener at all, so it sounds sincere.
It praises the pasta in a way that sounds false.

feedback.es: La broma apunta al esfuerzo del anfitrión y el suavizador final llega después del golpe: no consigue quitar el filo.

origin.text: Dear Tom, your pasta was so heavy that the table needed a rest, and you clearly believe that cooking is either an art or a test for your guests. No offence, of course.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Tanto mi teléfono como mi paraguas dejaron de funcionar.»

answer.text: Both my phone and my umbrella stopped working

feedback.es: Both… and une los dos sujetos y el verbo queda en plural: stopped working.

prompt.es: Escucha el comentario radiofónico: ¿por qué funciona la exageración de la columnista?

choices.text: It hides her real opinion of the train behind jokes she does not mean.
It expresses genuine tiredness without turning the complaint bitter.
It shows that commuters on her train really do swap birthdays.
It follows a rule from her editor that every column must contain a joke.

feedback.es: La exageración expresa un cansancio real sin volver amarga la queja: los chistes la suavizan y la regla del editor limita el daño.

origin.audio: In her column about public transport, the writer complains that her morning train is so crowded that she has learned to sleep standing up, that the train is such a tiny space that commuters exchange birthdays by the third stop, and that neither the conductor nor the timetable has ever told the truth. Readers love it, because nobody believes a word of it. The exaggeration is her way of saying that she is tired, and the jokes soften a complaint that might otherwise sound bitter. Her editor adds only one rule: never go too far, and never aim the joke at a person who could be hurt.

prompt.es: ¿Qué busca con la broma del comienzo quien responde a Sara?

choices.text: To turn the complaint into a joke so that it can be forgotten quickly.
To share the blame with the kitchen staff in a friendly way.
To keep the mood friendly while still taking the complaint seriously.
To avoid offering a solution by making the whole matter a joke.

feedback.es: La broma exagera el problema para acercarse a Sara, y el almuerzo gratis y el cierre serio demuestran que la queja sí se toma en serio.

origin.text: Dear Sara, I am sorry that your sandwich was cold. It was such a dramatic disaster that I have asked the kitchen to hold a minute of silence. Only joking: I have already arranged a free lunch for you, and I hope that this small gesture shows how seriously we take every complaint.

prompt.es: Completa: «Una sonrisa y un «solo bromeaba» pueden quitar filo a una queja.»

feedback.es: Take the edge off es la expresión fija para suavizar algo que resultaba demasiado duro.

origin.text: A quick smile and an “only joking” can ___ the edge off a sharp complaint. Without them, even a friendly exaggeration might sound like an attack.

prompt.es: Escribe una queja exagerada y la respuesta bromista de un amigo (180–240 palabras).

answer.text: My complaint is simple: the queue at the post office was so long that I learned to play the guitar while I waited. It was such a slow morning that the clocks went on strike, and both my patience and my shoes were worn out before I reached the window. Either the post office has forgotten how to count, or the staff are training to become statues. I am kind of upset, but I am only joking. My friend Leo answered at once: Poor you! You are so dramatic that the theatre should call you. Neither the queue nor the clerk deserves such an unfair review, but either you take a book next time, or I will bring you a chair. Only joking: come to my house, and I will make you a hot chocolate.
accepted: My complaint is simple: the queue at the post office was so long that I learned to play the guitar while I waited. It was such a slow morning that the clocks went on strike, and both my patience and my shoes were worn out before I reached the window. Either the post office has forgotten how to count, or the staff are training to become statues. I am kind of upset, but I am only joking. My friend Leo answered at once: Poor you! You are so dramatic that the theatre should call you. Neither the queue nor the clerk deserves such an unfair review, but either you take a book next time, or I will bring you a chair. Only joking: come to my house, and I will make you a hot chocolate.

Here is my complaint about the bus. The journey was so slow that I finished a whole novel, and the seat was such a hard seat that I now walk like a robot. Both my phone and my umbrella stopped working, and neither the driver nor the weather said sorry. Either the bus company has lost the map, or the driver is taking the scenic route around the planet. I am sort of tired, but I am just joking. My friend Mia replied: Poor you! You are so brave that you deserve a medal. Either you leave earlier, or I will buy you a bicycle. Only kidding. Come for dinner tonight, and I will cook pasta, so we can complain about the bus together.

feedback.es: Una respuesta completa exagera con so… that y such a…, reparte la queja con un correlativo y mantiene el buen tono con un suavizador.

origin.text: Escribe en inglés una queja exagerada sobre algo cotidiano (una cola, un atasco, un autobús) y la respuesta bromista de un amigo. Usa dos estructuras de intensidad (so… that y such a…), un correlativo (both… and, either… or o neither… nor) y un suavizador (kind of, only joking).

prompt.es: ¿Qué postura defiende el autor del blog sobre la exageración?

choices.text: It is a form of lying that speakers should avoid.
It is acceptable in every situation, between any two people.
It is acceptable whenever the speaker says that he is only joking.
It is acceptable when both sides know that it is not literal.

feedback.es: Antes la veía como mentira; ahora la entiende como un pacto: es aceptable mientras ambos saben que no es literal y el tema no hiere.

origin.text: I used to think that exaggeration was a form of lying. Now I see that it is a kind of contract: the speaker promises not to be taken literally, and the listener promises to laugh. The contract breaks only when the joke is about something that the other person cannot change, because then nobody is playing a game any more.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Ni el autobús ni el clima tuvieron la culpa.»

answer.text: Neither the bus nor the weather was to blame

feedback.es: Neither… nor concuerda con el sujeto más cercano (the weather) y el verbo va en afirmativo: was.

prompt.es: Escucha el mensaje de mi hermano: ¿qué queja es real y no una exageración?

choices.text: The length of the film he watched.
The price of the ice cream he bought.
The low temperature inside the cinema.

feedback.es: El helado congelado y los créditos eternos son hipérboles; el «kind of serious» revela que lo que de verdad le molestó fue el frío.

origin.audio: My brother sent me a complaint about the cinema. He said that the room was so cold that the ice cream froze, and that the film was so long that the credits felt like a holiday. Then he added that he was kind of serious about the cold, because he had to borrow a stranger's coat. I replied that he should bring one next time.

prompt.es: Lee el borrador de Leo: ¿qué broma debería quitar?

choices.text: The joke about Tom's age.
The joke about the wedding cake.
The joke about the coffee.

feedback.es: Las bromas sobre hábitos (tarde, generoso) son cariñosas; la de la edad es el tema que más fácilmente ofende y conviene cortarla.

hint.es: Piensa en qué rasgo no puede cambiar Tom.

origin.text: Leo's draft for Tom's birthday has three jokes. First: Tom is so late that he arrived at his own wedding after the cake. Second: Tom is so old that his birthday candles need a fire permit. Third: Tom is so generous that he pays for everybody's coffee.

prompt.es: Completa: «Una broma sobre su edad se pasaría de la raya.»

feedback.es: Cross the line es la expresión fija para pasarse del límite entre la broma cariñosa y la ofensiva.

hint.es: Verbo que significa atravesar un límite.

origin.text: Mia loves jokes about her terrible map-reading, but a joke about her age would ___ the line. Her brother knows exactly where it is.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada expresión del brindis con su función.

pairs.es: pasar del humor a la ofensa

feedback.es: Cada expresión marca un momento del brindis: bromear, suavizar, cerrar y evitar el exceso.

hint.es: Ordénalas mentalmente: primero bromeas, luego revisas, al final brindas.

pairs.es: pasar del humor a la ofensa

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿qué broma le pide su hermano que quite del brindis?

choices.text: The joke about how dangerous his cooking is.
The joke about how much money he makes.
The joke about losing his own birthday.

feedback.es: Se ríe de las bromas sobre su memoria y su cocina, pero pide que quite la del sueldo: es un tema personal que prefiere dejar fuera.

origin.audio: Mia read her draft toast to her brother. She had written that he was so forgetful that he once lost his own birthday, and that his cooking was such a danger to the neighbourhood that the firefighters knew his name. Her brother laughed, but he asked her to remove the line about his salary.

prompt.es: Lee la nota de la invitada: ¿qué opina del discurso?

choices.text: It was almost perfect, but too many jokes were about habits.
Part of it made some guests laugh but hurt another.
It was a success with all, including the grandmother.
It was almost perfect, but the grandmother should have laughed too.

feedback.es: Elogia el discurso («almost perfect»), pero señala que la broma sobre la edad hizo reír a los amigos y dejó incómoda a la abuela.

origin.text: Thanks for the speech, it was almost perfect. The joke about Tom's age got a big laugh from his friends, but his grandmother looked at her plate for the rest of the evening. Next time, perhaps we could keep the teasing for things that he can change.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Suaviza cualquier broma que pueda avergonzar al invitado.»

answer.text: Tone down any joke that might be embarrassing for the guest

feedback.es: Tone down lleva después el objeto (any joke) y una oración relativa que explica el riesgo.

prompt.es: Escucha el relato de la boda: ¿qué se deduce del silencio y de la reacción de la madre?

choices.text: That his mother disliked the earlier jokes as well as the last one.
That the speech ran long and the guests lost interest before the end.
That the line about the first wife crossed the line for the family.
That the best man had meant to upset the family on purpose.

feedback.es: Las bromas de hábitos funcionaron, pero la mención de la antigua novia provocó silencio y el gesto de la madre: esa línea fue la que se pasó de la raya.

origin.audio: At my cousin's wedding, the best man stood up with a card in one hand and a glass in the other. He began well: he said that my cousin was so generous that he had once given away his only umbrella in a storm, and so late for everything that his own wife had learned to tell him the wedding started an hour earlier. The guests laughed. Then he mentioned my cousin's first wife, and the room went quiet. My cousin's smile did not move, but his mother put down her glass. Afterwards the best man admitted that he had not read the room, and that one line had changed the whole evening.

prompt.es: ¿Qué le aconseja a Leo quien escribe el correo sobre su borrador?

choices.text: To delete the whole second page because it is too long for a toast.
To keep every joke, since Sara laughs at everything about herself.
To replace the cake joke with a more generous comment.
To keep the habit jokes and soften or cut the dress line.

feedback.es: Aprueba la broma del pastel porque Sara se ríe de ella, pero recomienda suavizar o eliminar la del vestido, que afecta algo que eligió con cuidado.

origin.text: Dear Leo, I have read your toast twice. The first page is lovely: the joke about Sara arriving after the cake is exactly the right kind of teasing, because she laughs at it herself. The second page worries me. The line about her dress might be funny to you, but I would tone it down, or leave it out, because she chose that dress with great care.

prompt.es: Completa: «Pidió a todos que alzaran una copa por la feliz pareja.»

feedback.es: Raise a glass es la expresión habitual para invitar a brindar al final de un discurso.

origin.text: After the last joke, the best man thanked the guests for their patience. Then he asked everybody to ___ a glass to the happy couple.

prompt.es: Escribe el brindis para Mia con bromas amables y una revisión (200–260 palabras).

answer.text: Friends and family, please raise a glass to Mia, who turns thirty today! Mia is so generous that she cooks dinner for the whole street, and she is so late for everything that she arrived at her own party after the cake. I am only joking: we would wait for her all night. She is kind of famous for her terrible maps, but she is such a good friend that we always follow her anyway. I had planned a joke about her age, but I have decided to cut it, because it could be embarrassing for her and it would not be fair. Instead, I want to say something sincere: thank you, Mia, for being the first person to call when things go wrong, and the last one to leave when they go right. We are lucky to have you. Cheers, Mia, and happy birthday!
accepted: Friends and family, please raise a glass to Mia, who turns thirty today! Mia is so generous that she cooks dinner for the whole street, and she is so late for everything that she arrived at her own party after the cake. I am only joking: we would wait for her all night. She is kind of famous for her terrible maps, but she is such a good friend that we always follow her anyway. I had planned a joke about her age, but I have decided to cut it, because it could be embarrassing for her and it would not be fair. Instead, I want to say something sincere: thank you, Mia, for being the first person to call when things go wrong, and the last one to leave when they go right. We are lucky to have you. Cheers, Mia, and happy birthday!

Dear friends, let us all raise a glass to Carlos on his fortieth birthday. He is so kind that he lends his car to anybody who asks, and he is so forgetful that he once looked for his phone while he was talking on it. I am just joking: we love him exactly as he is. Carlos is sort of a legend in the kitchen, but he is such a funny cook that we always eat before we arrive. I wrote a joke about his money, and I will not read it, because it would be unfair and it could hurt people who love him. Thank you, Carlos, for every good day, and for always being the first person to help when something goes wrong. Cheers to Carlos, and happy birthday!

feedback.es: Un brindis completo tiene bromas amables con so/such… that, un suavizador, la revisión visible de lo que se retira y un cierre sincero.

Only then did a friend explain that brave, in that tone, means “probably a mistake”. Since then I listen to what people do not say as carefully as to what they do.

origin.audio: A researcher interviewed on a podcast recently described what she calls the airport effect. A traveller spends two hours in a foreign airport, meets three tired officials and decides that the whole country is unfriendly. The mistake, she says, is not in noticing a pattern, but in announcing it as a law. By and large, she added, people tend to be helpful when they are not exhausted. If you must generalise, leave room for the exceptions, because the exceptions are usually the people who change your mind. Her listeners laughed, but many wrote in afterwards to say that they had been guilty of the airport effect themselves.

Only after a week did the mother say, over tea, that in their house guests are expected to serve themselves, and that asking is not needed. Marta burst out laughing, and so did everyone else. In other countries people tend to cut the cake first, whereas we do it the right way.
Everybody in my family always sings first, unlike all other countries.

feedback.es: Tend to y whereas describen la diferencia sin juicio; las otras opciones, aunque usen las mismas estructuras, declaran una costumbre correcta o universal.

origin.text: A student is explaining to an exchange student how her family celebrates birthdays. She wants to describe the difference without sounding better than anybody else, and she is looking for the best sentence to use.

prompt.es: Ordena: «En general, los visitantes son bienvenidos a nuestra mesa.»

answer.text: By and large, visitors are welcome at our table

feedback.es: By and large abre la frase y matiza; visitors are welcome at our table es la generalización.

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿qué quiere transmitir quien habla al describir las costumbres de su casa?

choices.text: That visitors should copy her customs as soon as they arrive.
That her mother's kitchen rules are stricter than other families' rules.
That habits which look odd are gestures of welcome with their own logic.
That cooking together is a better custom than cooking alone.

feedback.es: Cada hábito que sorprende resulta ser un gesto de bienvenida con su lógica; la comparación final, «neither way is better», evita juzgar.

origin.audio: When visitors first come to my house, they usually notice three things: the shoes by the door, the very long goodbye and the fact that my mother will not let anyone help in the kitchen. At first glance these habits may strike them as strange. By and large, however, they leave understanding that each one is a gesture of welcome: the shoes keep the floor clean for the children, the long goodbye shows that nobody is in a hurry, and the empty kitchen is my mother's way of saying that a guest is a guest. Whereas in my friend's home everybody cooks together, in ours the cook is the host. Neither way is better; both are ways of saying: you matter.

prompt.es: ¿Qué corrección propone quien revisa el borrador?

choices.text: Delete the shared dish example because it is too personal.
Remove every comparison with other countries from the paragraph.
Soften “cold” to “a bit cold” so that the generalisation sounds fairer.
Replace the judgement by a description of behaviour.

feedback.es: Elogia el ejemplo y el tono cálido, pero el juicio «cold» sobre otras personas debe sustituirse por lo que hacen: describir conductas, no rasgos.

origin.text: Your paragraph about Sunday lunch is warm and vivid, and the example of the shared dish works well. However, the sentence “In other countries people are cold at meals” is an unfair generalisation, and it undermines the respectful tone of the rest. A better comparison would describe what people do, not what they are.

prompt.es: Completa: «En algunas casas es costumbre quitarse los zapatos al entrar.»

feedback.es: It is customary to + verbo base es la fórmula de registro más formal para «es costumbre».

origin.text: Guests do not always know the rules of a new house, but in some homes it is ___ to take off your shoes at the door, and a polite visitor does it without being asked.

prompt.es: Explica una costumbre de tu familia a un visitante (180–240 palabras).

answer.text: In my family, Friday dinner is a long-standing tradition. By and large, everybody is home by seven, and the children tend to choose the menu. For example, last week my little brother asked for rice and chicken, and we all agreed. A visitor is always welcome, and guests usually bring a dessert or a small gift. It is customary to share one big dish from the centre of the table, which may strike a visitor as unusual at first. In many countries each person has a separate plate, whereas in mine we pass the food around and talk while we eat. Neither way is better; each custom makes sense at home. Please do not worry if you are unsure what to do: my mother will show you, and she will give you a warm welcome. I hope that you can join us one Friday.
accepted: In my family, Friday dinner is a long-standing tradition. By and large, everybody is home by seven, and the children tend to choose the menu. For example, last week my little brother asked for rice and chicken, and we all agreed. A visitor is always welcome, and guests usually bring a dessert or a small gift. It is customary to share one big dish from the centre of the table, which may strike a visitor as unusual at first. In many countries each person has a separate plate, whereas in mine we pass the food around and talk while we eat. Neither way is better; each custom makes sense at home. Please do not worry if you are unsure what to do: my mother will show you, and she will give you a warm welcome. I hope that you can join us one Friday.

Every Sunday my family has lunch at my grandmother's house, a custom that is older than I am. As a rule, everybody arrives around noon, and the younger cousins tend to arrive last. For instance, last month my uncle brought a cake that he had baked himself, and we all laughed because it was still warm. Visitors are welcome too, and they usually sit next to my grandmother. In some countries people eat quickly and leave, whereas in mine the table is a place to stay and talk for hours. Neither way is wrong; each custom simply suits its own home. It may seem unusual at first, but guests quickly feel at ease. I would love to see you there one Sunday.

feedback.es: Un texto completo presenta la costumbre, matiza dos generalizaciones, da un ejemplo concreto y compara con respeto, sin juzgar.

origin.text: Explica a un visitante extranjero una costumbre de tu familia (la cena del viernes, el almuerzo del domingo…). Escribe en inglés con dos generalizaciones matizadas (by and large, tend to…), un ejemplo concreto y una comparación respetuosa con otra costumbre.

prompt.es: ¿Cuál es la postura de quien escribe sobre explicar una costumbre a un extraño?

choices.text: Explaining a custom values it and welcomes strangers.
Explaining a custom makes it sound less natural, so it is best avoided.
Only customs that are very old deserve an explanation.
Strangers should learn the customs without asking questions.

feedback.es: Rebate la idea del museo: explicar con cariño mantiene viva la costumbre y abre la puerta al extraño.

origin.text: Some people claim that explaining a custom to a stranger makes it sound less natural, as if we were showing our family in a museum. I see it differently. A custom that we cannot explain is one that we have stopped noticing, and describing it kindly is a way of keeping it alive and of inviting the stranger in.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Mientras que nosotros compartimos un plato, ellos usan platos separados.»

answer.text: Whereas we share one dish, they use separate plates
accepted: Whereas we share one dish, they use separate plates
They use separate plates, whereas we share one dish

feedback.es: Whereas une dos hechos contrastados; puede abrir la frase o ir en medio, separado por coma.

prompt.es: Escucha el mensaje: ¿qué actitud muestra Ana al explicar la costumbre?

choices.text: Formal: she lists conditions that Tom must accept to be welcome.
Relaxed and welcoming: she explains a habit, not a demand.
Nervous: she worries that Tom will dislike her family's customs.
Defensive: she justifies her family's habits before Tom can judge them.

feedback.es: Dice «not a rule, just a habit» y ofrece una solución si olvida algo: explica una costumbre con calidez y sin imponerla.

origin.audio: Hi Tom, it is Ana. About Saturday: at our house we tend to take off our shoes at the door, so bring some warm socks. It is not a rule, just a habit, and my mother will lend you some if you forget. She would be very happy if you tried her dessert, which is an old family recipe.

prompt.es: Lee el intercambio: ¿por qué es diplomática la respuesta de Sara?

choices.text: It avoids the question by changing the subject quickly.
It admits that the family is unfriendly to every guest.
It welcomes the question and avoids absolute words.

feedback.es: Sara reconoce la pregunta con «Good question!» y responde con by and large y una razón concreta, sin absolutos ni evasivas.

hint.es: Fíjate en cómo empieza su respuesta y en las palabras que evita.

origin.text: Carlos, a guest from abroad, asks his hosts why nobody talks during dinner. Sara smiles and answers, “Good question! By and large we talk a lot, but tonight we were all very tired.” Carlos laughs, and the silence disappears.

prompt.es: Completa: «Ana preparó té para despejar el ambiente.»

feedback.es: Clear the air es la expresión fija para disipar la tensión tras una discusión o un malentendido.

hint.es: Sustantivo que respiramos.

origin.text: After the argument at dinner, nobody wanted to speak first, so Ana made tea to clear the ___ between them and offer a fresh start.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada expresión del anfitrión con su función.

feedback.es: Cada expresión cumple un papel distinto al recibir a un invitado: aclarar, suavizar, acoger y responder con tacto.

hint.es: Piensa en el orden de una visita: bienvenida, malentendido, pregunta.

prompt.es: Escucha: ¿qué hizo especialmente bien el padre al contestar a la invitada?

choices.text: He explained the habit but insisted that the guest must follow it.
He explained the habit and offered to adapt it if the guest preferred.
He offered to change the habit without explaining why it exists.
He apologised for the habit and promised to abandon it for good.

feedback.es: Reconoce la pregunta, describe el hábito con «tend to» y se ofrece a adaptarlo: así la invitada se siente en casa.

origin.audio: Our guest from Canada arrived on Friday and asked why we never eat before eight. My father said, “Good question. Most families here tend to eat late, but it is only a habit, and we can eat earlier if you prefer.” The guest looked relieved. She said later that nobody had ever answered her so kindly, and that she felt at home by the end of the evening.

prompt.es: Lee el mensaje: ¿qué busca quien lo escribe?

choices.text: To excuse the family by proving that the guest was in the wrong.
To ask the guest to follow the customs of the house from now on.
To clear the air by explaining the custom kindly.
To cancel the invitation politely without saying so.

feedback.es: Se disculpa, explica la costumbre (la cocinera come la última) y deja la puerta abierta a más preguntas, sin culpar al invitado.

origin.text: I apologise for what happened at dinner. We did not mean to leave you out; in our house the cook eats last and the guests start first, so we assumed that you would begin. Please tell me if anything else surprises you.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Por favor, siéntete como en casa y pregúntame lo que quieras.»

answer.text: Please feel at home and ask me anything

feedback.es: Feel at home es una expresión fija; ask me anything invita al invitado a preguntar sin reservas.

prompt.es: Escucha el relato: ¿cómo arregla la familia la situación con Jamal?

choices.text: By asking Jamal to explain why he had not slept well that night.
By removing the house rules and inviting him to write his own list.
By telling Jamal politely that a second blanket was not really needed.
By saying sorry for the joke, making clear the list was no order and giving him a blanket.

feedback.es: La familia se disculpa por la broma, aclara que la lista no era una orden y ofrece la manta sin comentarios: reparar sin culpar.

origin.audio: When Jamal, an exchange student from Kenya, came to stay with us, my mother gave him a list of house rules, which was the first mistake. The second was my father's joke that only tourists ask for a second blanket. Jamal smiled politely, but the next morning he looked tired. My mother, who reads faces well, took me aside and suggested that we apologise for the joke, clarify that the list was not an order, and offer a blanket without comment. At breakfast my father said, with a smile, that he had been a bad host and a worse performer. Jamal laughed, accepted the blanket, and asked whether the house rules included the recipe for my mother's bread.

prompt.es: ¿Qué busca quien escribe al responder así a la pregunta incómoda de Hana?

choices.text: To reply frankly to a difficult question, limited to what the writer knows.
To avoid the question by praising the families the writer knows.
To prove that every family in the town is quieter than Hana's.
To apologise because the writer's family is so different from Hana's.

feedback.es: Acota («only speak for the families I know»), matiza con «many» y «tend to» y explica sin disculparse: una respuesta sincera y sin absolutos.

origin.text: Dear Hana, you asked whether all the families in our town are as quiet as mine. It is a good question, and I should say first that I can only speak for the families I know. Many of them tend to be reserved at dinner, but others are noisy, particularly on Sundays. Please do not take our quiet as a sign that we are cold; it is simply how we were brought up.

prompt.es: Completa: «Déjame aclarar lo que pasó anoche.»

feedback.es: Set the record straight es la expresión fija para corregir una impresión equivocada.

origin.text: I did not mean to be rude when we started eating without you, so let me set the record ___ about what happened last night.

prompt.es: Da la bienvenida a tu invitado, aclara y responde con tacto (200–260 palabras).

answer.text: Welcome, Carlos, and please feel at home! In my family we tend to eat dinner at six, and by and large everybody helps to set the table. Let me clarify something about last night: we did not mean to be rude when we started eating without you. I apologise, because I should have explained that we usually do not wait after seven. You asked a good question: why do we not talk more at dinner? It is a fair thing to wonder, and I will try to answer tactfully. Some families are quieter, and ours likes to enjoy the food first, whereas in your country people seem to talk more. Neither way is better, and it is only a habit; nobody is upset. Tomorrow we will talk as much as you like, and I will show you the city. No offence if we are quiet again on Sunday: my grandmother cooks, and we tend to listen to her stories.
accepted: Welcome, Carlos, and please feel at home! In my family we tend to eat dinner at six, and by and large everybody helps to set the table. Let me clarify something about last night: we did not mean to be rude when we started eating without you. I apologise, because I should have explained that we usually do not wait after seven. You asked a good question: why do we not talk more at dinner? It is a fair thing to wonder, and I will try to answer tactfully. Some families are quieter, and ours likes to enjoy the food first, whereas in your country people seem to talk more. Neither way is better, and it is only a habit; nobody is upset. Tomorrow we will talk as much as you like, and I will show you the city. No offence if we are quiet again on Sunday: my grandmother cooks, and we tend to listen to her stories.

Hello, Hana, make yourself at home! As a rule, my family has breakfast together at eight, and we tend to be quiet because we are still sleepy. Let me explain something about this morning: we did not mean to ignore you when we stayed silent. I am sorry, because I should have told you about our custom. That is a fair question: why is nobody talking at the table? In some houses people talk a lot at breakfast, whereas in ours we like silence and coffee first. It is only a habit, and nobody is upset. At lunch we will talk as much as you like, and I promise to ask you about your country and your family. I hope that you will feel at ease with us very soon.

feedback.es: El texto da la bienvenida, explica costumbres con matices, aclara el malentendido sin culpar y responde con tacto a la pregunta.

origin.text: Tu invitado Carlos llega de otro país. Escribe en inglés: da la bienvenida, explica dos costumbres con matices (tend to, by and large), aclara un malentendido (por ejemplo, que empezaron a comer sin él) con Let me clarify… y responde con tacto a su pregunta: «Why do you not talk more at dinner?».

evidenceGroups: let me set the record straight

prompt.es: ¿Cuál es la actitud de quien escribe ante los invitados de otros países?

choices.text: Guests should accept every habit of the host without asking.
Open explanation and questions are better than guessing what offends.
It is wiser to avoid inviting people from other countries.
Hosts should leave every guest alone to avoid any problem.

feedback.es: Ya no adivina qué ofende: explica sus hábitos y pregunta por los del invitado, una estrategia sin coste que evita casi todo el daño.

origin.text: Hosting a foreigner taught me that politeness has no universal grammar. Some guests want to be left alone; others think that being left alone means being ignored. I used to worry that every choice would offend someone. Now I explain my habits openly and ask about theirs, which costs nothing and avoids most of the damage.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Déjame aclarar lo que no quisimos decir.»

answer.text: Let me clarify what we did not mean to say

feedback.es: Let me clarify + what + oración: aclara la intención sin culpar a nadie.

prompt.es: Escucha el mensaje del invitado: ¿qué quiere transmitir?

choices.text: That the guest was offended by the question about the guest's country.
That the guest regrets having accepted the invitation.
That the guest enjoyed the evening and feels comfortable with the family.
That the guest thinks the family talks too much at dinner.

feedback.es: Agradece la velada, resta importancia a su respuesta larga y cierra con un proverbio que muestra que se siente a gusto.

origin.audio: Thank you for the lovely evening. Your question about my country was not awkward at all, although I am afraid my answer was too long. Please tell me if I talk too much. Back home we say that a guest who is shy at the start is a guest who will be very happy in the end.

prompt.es: Localiza la concesión: ¿qué reconoce la hablante antes de girar?

choices.text: That a ringing phone can pull attention away from a lesson.
That a locker system deserves a one-term trial in this school.
That phones ruin concentration in every lesson, as some teachers claim.

feedback.es: La concesión llega antes de «That said»: admite que una pantalla que vibra distrae; el ensayo con taquillas es lo que propone ella y arruinar la concentración es lo que alegan otros.

hint.es: La concesión es lo que admite antes del giro, no lo que defiende después.

origin.text: Some teachers argue that phones ruin concentration, and I grant you that a ringing phone can distract from a lesson. That said, our school has never tried a simple locker system, so nobody can claim it failed. On balance, I would like to see it tested for one term.

prompt.es: Completa: «Te doy la razón: puede serlo, pero la oficina tiene un teléfono gratuito.»

feedback.es: I grant you that… es la fórmula de concesión generosa; concede no admite «you» detrás.

hint.es: Verbo que significa «admitir, dar la razón»; empieza por g.

origin.text: Some pupils say a phone is a lifeline after dark. I ___ you that it can be, but the office phone is free to use.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Es un punto válido, pero la norma sigue en pie.»

answer.text: That is a valid point but the rule still stands

feedback.es: La concesión (valid point) va primero y el giro con but introduce lo que se defiende.

hint.es: Primero la concesión, después but y tu postura.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué concede la hablante sobre las clases con celular.

choices.text: That a dictionary check is a poor reason to allow phones.
That some pupils do waste whole lessons staring at their own screens.
That a traffic-light system would be unfair to teachers.

feedback.es: «I accept that some pupils stare at their screens…» es la concesión; «Even so» abre la refutación y el semáforo es su propuesta.

origin.audio: Ms Reyes says phones should stay in bags all day. I see where she is coming from, and I accept that some pupils stare at their screens for an entire lesson. Even so, a blanket rule punishes those who use a phone to check a dictionary. She could try a traffic-light system instead, with green for research and red for silence.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada frase del debate con la función que cumple.

pairs: Admittedly, the rule is easy to explain
That said, it is hard to enforce
On balance, I would keep it
That argument does not hold water
One phone rang during the test

feedback.es: Cada marcador cumple un papel: Admittedly concede, that said gira, on balance cierra, hold water descarta y one phone rang ilustra.

pairs: Admittedly, the rule is easy to explain

prompt.es: ¿Qué defiende realmente Tom en este resumen de su intervención?

choices.text: That phones in emergencies are so important that no rule should limit them.
That pupils who use phones sensibly should be punished along with the rest.
That the ban is reasonable because pupils can already phone home from school.

feedback.es: Tom concede el valor del celular en una emergencia, pero lo que defiende es que la prohibición es razonable porque ya existe otra vía.

origin.text: Tom's speech opened with a concession: phones do let pupils reach home in an emergency. He then turned sharply, pointing out that the same pupils already have access to the school office. His closing line was more cautious, suggesting only that the ban should be reviewed after one term.

prompt.es: Escucha el fragmento y elige qué concede Leo antes de su giro.

choices.text: That a newcomer might depend on a translation app.
That most pupils use translation apps to cheat in tests.
That Mia had used a translation app herself at school.
That Mia's point deserved more attention than it had received.

feedback.es: La concesión es la generosidad inicial hacia el punto de Mia: un alumno recién llegado puede depender de la aplicación; lo demás es una generalización, un dato no mencionado o una opinión que Leo no expresa.

origin.audio: At Tuesday's debate, Leo argued for keeping phones in bags. He opened generously: Mia's point about translation apps was fair, he said, and he could see how a pupil new to the country might rely on one. Even so, he went on, the same app can write a whole essay in seconds, and teachers cannot tell the difference from across the room. He did not claim that every pupil cheats; he said only that a rule has to work for the pupils who do. On balance, he thought a ban in tests and a free hand in practice lessons was the honest middle ground, although he admitted the school might struggle to enforce it.

prompt.es: Escucha de nuevo: ¿qué actitud muestra Leo hacia su propia propuesta final?

choices.text: He presents it as a perfect answer that leaves nothing more to discuss.
He offers a fair compromise but admits it may be hard to apply.
He proposes it reluctantly and would drop it the moment teachers object.
He sees it as a fair compromise that most teachers will gladly welcome.

feedback.es: Leo llama «honest middle ground» a su propuesta, pero admite que aplicarla puede costar: actitud de compromiso realista, no de certeza ni de desgana.

origin.audio: At Tuesday's debate, Leo argued for keeping phones in bags. prompt.es: Completa: «La directora estaba dispuesta a conceder que la norma era confusa.»

feedback.es: Concede that… es la colocación natural para reconocer un punto ajeno sin cambiar la postura; los sinónimos admit o accept también encajan.

origin.text: The head teacher was prepared to ___ that the old rule had been unclear. She would not, however, drop it completely, and she asked the council to give it one more term.

prompt.es: Escribe una concesión y una refutación sobre traductores en exámenes.

answer.text: I grant you that a translation app can help newcomers; that said, in a test it would be unfair to pupils who have learned the words.
accepted: I grant you that a translation app can help newcomers; that said, in a test it would be unfair to pupils who have learned the words.
Admittedly, a translation app helps pupils who are new to the country; nevertheless, in an exam it would be unfair to those who have studied the words.
I concede that an app can help newcomers, but in a test it would be unfair to pupils who have learned the vocabulary.

feedback.es: Una buena respuesta concede con una fórmula (I grant you, admittedly, I concede) y gira después hacia la postura propia.

origin.text: Concede que un traductor ayuda a los alumnos recién llegados y rebate que en un examen sería injusto para quienes han estudiado las palabras.

prompt.es: ¿Con qué propósito escribe Sara este correo a la dirección?

choices.text: To drop the council's objection now that she understands the rule.
To accuse the staff of ignoring what the survey of pupils clearly shows.
To ask for a delay so that the council's findings can be considered.
To propose that the ban apply at break but not in lessons, as pupils prefer.

feedback.es: Sara reconoce la postura del centro, pero su petición es esperar a los resultados completos: busca aplazar, no retirar ni acusar.

origin.text: Dear Head Teacher, thank you for meeting the pupil council. I understand why you want a single rule, and I do not doubt that staff are under pressure. All the same, our survey suggests that most pupils would accept a ban in lessons but not at break. I would therefore ask you to hold off on the outright ban until we have shared the full results next week.

prompt.es: Ordena: «En conjunto, el argumento a favor de la prohibición no se sostiene.»

answer.text: On balance the case for a ban does not hold water
accepted: On balance the case for a ban does not hold water
The case for a ban does not hold water on balance

feedback.es: On balance abre una valoración global y does not hold water descarta el argumento.

prompt.es: Completa: «La última razón, francamente, no se sostenía.»

feedback.es: Hold water (o hold up) describe un argumento que resiste el examen; Carlos debió conceder que el cuarto no lo hacía.

origin.text: Carlos listed four reasons for the ban. The first three were strong; the last one, frankly, did not hold ___. He should have conceded as much.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Por mucho que valoremos la biblioteca, no podemos pagar la cuota.»

answer.text: Much as we value the library we cannot pay the fee
accepted: Much as we value the library we cannot pay the fee
We cannot pay the fee much as we value the library

feedback.es: Much as + sujeto + verbo abre la concesión y la postura sigue sin but; el orden inverso también es natural.

hint.es: Empieza por Much as y no añadas but.

prompt.es: Completa: «Por pequeña que suene, sigue siendo una subida del veinte por ciento.»

feedback.es: Tras However va el adjetivo, luego el sujeto y el verbo: However small it may sound equivale a «por pequeña que suene».

origin.text: The bus company calls the new fare a small adjustment. ___ small it may sound, it is still a rise of twenty per cent for people on low incomes.

choices.text: Generous though sounds the offer, it comes at a cost.
Generous though the offer sounds, it comes at a cost.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige la actitud de la hablante hacia el plan de la biblioteca.

On the side of the architects, who she feels have been unfairly blamed for the cost.

origin.audio: Much as the residents admire the new library, they cannot ignore what it will cost them. However popular the plan is, it will raise their bills by eight per cent. Generous though the architects have been, and for all that the building is lovely, nobody has explained who will pay for the repairs.

prompt.es: Completa: «Por mucho dinero que recaude, el techo no se reparará antes del invierno.»

feedback.es: However much + nombre no contable (money) equivale a «por mucho dinero que»; con nombres contables usarías however many.

answer.text: However clever the plan is it will come at a cost
accepted: However clever the plan is it will come at a cost
It will come at a cost however clever the plan is

prompt.es: Escucha la noticia y elige por qué la líder rechaza conservar la piscina vieja.

The volunteers had stopped looking after the old building.

I believe that pupils should clean their classroom every week. I concede that it takes time from lessons, and some parents think the school should do it. origin.audio: A lecturer is explaining why she doubts a headline. The headline said: rapid adoption of the app triggers a significant reduction in waste. She points out that the sentence is tidy and convincing, but that it conceals everything a careful reader needs to know. Who adopted the app, and how quickly? Waste of what, and measured by whom? She does not say the claim is false. Her point is that nominalisation lets a writer present a hopeful result as if it were simply a fact, so a reader must unpack the noun phrases before trusting the headline.

prompt.es: ¿Qué valoración del experimento es la más precisa?

choices.text: Flawed: a single trial with volunteers can never show anything.
Tentative: a small first trial that hints at a possible benefit.

feedback.es: El equipo realizó el experimento una sola vez, con treinta voluntarios, y pide un ensayo mayor: es un resultado provisional, no concluyente.

origin.text: Reviewer's report: The authors have plainly worked hard. Their survey is thorough, and their statistics are handled with care. Yet the headline claim, that green tea improves concentration, rests on a single classroom in one school, with no comparison group. prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué quiere enseñar la profesora sobre cómo valorar un estudio pequeño.

choices.text: That a judgement is fair only when the claim is no bigger than the evidence.
That a small sample is an acceptable reason to call any study flawed.

feedback.es: La profesora dice que un estudio pequeño puede ser honesto si sus afirmaciones son prudentes; el fallo está en la distancia entre evidencia y afirmación.

origin.audio: When you evaluate a study, do not reach for the strongest word. Calling a study flawed because its sample is small is fair only if the authors claim more than that sample allows. A small study that says tentative things can be perfectly honest. Suppose two teams each test forty people. One team writes that the medicine always works; the other writes that the result is encouraging and deserves a larger trial. Their data may be the same, and yet only the first team has gone too far. The real fault is a claim that is bigger than its evidence.

origin.text: Five years ago, the city council decided to build more than one hundred kilometres of protected bike lanes. At first, many residents opposed the plan, and shop owners were especially worried, because they assumed that fewer parking places would mean fewer customers. However, the figures published this spring tell a different story. The proportion of people who cycle to work has risen from three per cent to eleven per cent, while car traffic in the centre has fallen by nine per cent. Air quality has improved, the main streets are quieter, and several schools report that more pupils now arrive by bicycle. The researcher who led the study argues that the investment has already paid for itself, because the city now spends less on road repairs and on health care. She points out that sales in the shops along the new lanes have grown by six per cent. Nevertheless, some critics claim that the results for small shops are unreliable, since only forty businesses answered the survey. The researcher acknowledges this limitation, and she suggests that the council should repeat the survey next year with a larger sample. Meanwhile, the council hopes to build more lanes in the north of the city, although it has not yet said who will pay for them.

origin.audio: In the third chapter, the narrator describes her brother's wedding in loving detail: the flowers, the music, the speeches. She mentions, almost in passing, that she left before the cake was cut, and that her mother did not speak to her for a month afterwards. She never explains why. Readers who accept her warm tone at face value will miss the gap. Because the most important moment of the whole day is the one she skips, we are invited to suspect that her own behaviour was the reason for the silence.

answer.text: The Quiet Harbour follows a woman who returns to her fishing village after ten years and finds that nobody wants to talk about the night her father disappeared. From the first scene, the film is gripping: the camera stays on faces, and every silence seems to hide something. The cast is excellent, and the young lead almost steals the show. Her brother must have known more than he admits, because he never looks at her during the wedding, and the old neighbour, who says she never left her house, can't have stayed in that night, since her boots were covered in mud. The dialogue is convincing, for example in the kitchen scene, where two sentences reveal a whole family history. The one flaw is the pacing: the final twist feels rushed, and the ending may fall short of the promise of the first hour. Even so, I would highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys a slow, thoughtful mystery.

The Quiet Harbour is about a woman who goes back to her village by the sea after ten years. The film is stunning to look at and the actors are very good. Her brother must have hidden something from her, because he avoids her eyes at the wedding. The neighbour can't have stayed at home that night, since her boots were full of mud. The dialogue feels real, for instance in the kitchen scene, where a few words explain the whole family. The main weakness is that the story is predictable and the ending is rushed, so it falls short of its beginning. Nevertheless, I recommend it to everybody who likes slow films with a mystery, because the performances alone are worth the ticket.

answer.text: I would argue that the ending of The Blue Door is ambiguous on purpose. The narrator says that nobody ever lived in the house, but he can't have been honest, because he also says that his sister left after an argument. The wet letter is a clue: she must have been upset when she wrote it, and he might have kept it hidden for years. A plausible reading is that the blue door is a symbol of a memory that he cannot close. Carlos argues that the narrator is simply lying to us, and I concede that this is possible. However, I take issue with the idea that one lie spoils the whole book, and I am not entirely convinced that the writer wants us to be certain. But we should not read too much into one lie. The imagery of cold and rain makes the sadness resonate, and the ending stays open to interpretation. We will have to agree to disagree, Carlos.

In my reading, the last scene is ambiguous, and the blue door is a symbol of memory. The narrator can't have been telling the whole truth, because the letter was wet, so somebody must have read it or hidden it. His sister might have left in anger, and he might have closed the door to forget her. Carlos says that the narrator is lying, and I concede that this is plausible, because the clues contradict him. answer.text: Sunday. I landed at nine, and the taxi driver talked for the whole ride. I was completely knackered, so I went straight to bed. Monday. The thing is, I could not figure out the bus timetable. I asked a stranger to rephrase her directions twice, and apparently the bus was the wrong one anyway. Bummer! Wednesday. I managed to sort out my phone contract. To be honest, I pretty much guessed the forms, but no worries, the assistant was kind. Thursday. Culture shock hit me. I could not get the hang of tipping, and I felt bewildered in a restaurant full of people shouting. Saturday. It drizzled all day, so I stayed in and wrote this diary. Mind you, I am starting to settle in, and I can finally catch up on sleep. Anyway, it was a bustling, awesome week.

Mind you, I am starting to settle in, and I can finally catch up on sleep. Anyway, it was a bustling, awesome week.

Monday. I landed late, and the airport was chaos. On Tuesday I could not figure out the ticket machine, so I asked a man to rephrase what he was saying, and we muddled through with gestures. Bummer, I missed my bus! On Wednesday, to be honest, I felt homesick, but I managed to sort out my room with the landlady. Thursday. I am slowly getting the hang of the coffee shop, and the waiter says my accent is nice. Mind you, he says it to everybody. By Saturday I had pretty much settled in, and on Sunday I slept until noon. Anyway, it was a tiring but awesome first week. On Friday, a neighbour invited me for tea, and I could only make out half of what she said, but I got the gist of it, and we had a lovely evening.

feedback.es: Un buen diario ordena los días, combina bloques del habla con coloquialismos y deja ver una estrategia de comunicación.

origin.text: Escribe el diario de tu primera semana en un país nuevo (al menos 125 palabras; ideal, 200): ordena los días (On Monday…), usa tres bloques (figure out, sort out, get the hang of, settle in, muddle through…), dos expresiones coloquiales (to be honest, mind you, bummer…) y una estrategia de comunicación (pedir que lo reformulen).

To be honest, this is the third problem this month, and I am beginning to think that the plumber is the least of it. Anyway, bear with me: I will get to the bottom of it and call you on Monday at the latest.

To complain that the agency has already broken a promise.

origin.audio: Let me begin with an embarrassing story. Three years ago, I was on a stage very like this one, and my first slide read: Welcome, today I will talk about planning your week. Within a minute, half the room was looking at their phones. Why? Because I had opened with information, not with a reason to care. So tonight I will do it differently. Nine out of ten listeners forget a talk within a week, and I want you to be the exception. First, I will show you one mistake. Then I will give you a simple repair.

feedback.es: Al pedir que sean «la excepción», sugiere que quiere que recuerden la charla, frente a los nueve que la olvidan.

origin.text: Speakers are often advised to open gently, with a greeting, a thank-you and a few polite remarks. I would argue that the advice is a mistake. A cautious start may feel respectful, but it gives a bored audience no reason to stay, and by the time the real argument begins, attention has already drifted away.

She values them mainly because a surprising number is easy to remember later.

feedback.es: Concede que la cifra sorprende, pero solo la valora si el orador explica su relevancia: una aprobación condicionada.

origin.text: A surprising figure can be a fine opening gambit, but only if the speaker tells us at once why it matters. Otherwise, the number hangs in the air like a joke without an ending, and the audience admires it briefly before forgetting it.

origin.audio: Who has never forgotten a name the moment it was spoken? Nobody in this room, I suspect. First, I will explain why it happens: we are so busy preparing our own reply that we stop listening. Moreover, most of us never repeat the name aloud, which is the one habit that helps. Having said that, there is no need to feel guilty, because memory is not a skill we were ever trained to use. Moving on, let me briefly offer a simple technique, and then I will recap the whole idea in one sentence.

He is understanding: he treats it as a common habit, not a fault.
He is encouraging, but he thinks only trained public speakers can ever improve.

feedback.es: Explica el olvido como un hábito común y declara que no hay motivo de culpa: una actitud comprensiva, no acusadora.

origin.text: Advice columns love the rhetorical question. Who could possibly object to a little curiosity? Yet a speaker who asks three of them in a row sounds less like a guide than like a teacher giving an exam, and listeners soon notice that none of the questions is ever answered.

prompt.es: Escribe el centro de una charla con inversión, regla de tres y pregunta retórica.

answer.text: Every morning, millions of us do the same thing. We turn on the tap, we wait for the water to warm up, and we let it run. Who has ever counted how many litres disappear in those two minutes? Nobody, I suspect. Never have we had so much clean water, yet rarely do we treat it with respect. Not only do we waste water at home, but we also waste the energy that heats it. Here is what I suggest: three simple habits. First, keep a bowl in the shower. Second, turn off the tap while you brush your teeth. Third, repair every leak this week. Little did I know that three small habits would cut our bill by a third. Under no circumstances should we wait for a crisis, because water that has gone cannot be replaced. So tomorrow morning, turn off the tap, hold the bowl and feel what a difference it makes.
accepted: Every morning, millions of us do the same thing. We turn on the tap, we wait for the water to warm up, and we let it run. Who has ever counted how many litres disappear in those two minutes? Nobody, I suspect. Never have we had so much clean water, yet rarely do we treat it with respect. Not only do we waste water at home, but we also waste the energy that heats it. Here is what I suggest: three simple habits. First, keep a bowl in the shower. Second, turn off the tap while you brush your teeth. Third, repair every leak this week. Little did I know that three small habits would cut our bill by a third. Under no circumstances should we wait for a crisis, because water that has gone cannot be replaced. So tomorrow morning, turn off the tap, hold the bowl and feel what a difference it makes.

Think about the last time you left a tap running. Why did you do it? Because nobody ever told you that it matters. Seldom have we been asked to think about water, and rarely do we wonder where it goes. Not until a dry summer arrives do most of us notice. So let me give you three rules that cost nothing. First, take shorter showers. Second, use the washing machine only when it is full. Third, fix every leak at once. Little did my neighbours believe that these three rules could save a thousand litres a month, yet that is exactly what happened on our street. At no point should we say that one person cannot make a difference, because every street is made of people like you and me. So when you go home tonight, look at your tap, and ask yourself one thing: what will I change first?

answer.text: Quick question: how many of you have ever lost a tennis match to a ten-year-old? I have, and it changed my life. Three years ago, I was a beginner at our neighbourhood tennis club, and I wanted to quit after one week. Today I will tell you why I stayed. First, tennis taught me patience: I learned to wait before I move. Moreover, the club gave me friends who explained every mistake without laughing. Having said that, nobody ever made me feel small. Second, tennis changed how I deal with problems at work. Seldom have I felt so calm under pressure. Third, it costs almost nothing. You only need a ball and a friend. To sum up, be patient, be curious and never stop trying. That is my takeaway. And remember the ten-year-old? Last week, I beat her. Thank you for your question: you asked whether you must be good to join. Not at all; beginners are the heart of our club.

Second, tennis changed how I deal with problems at work. Seldom have I felt so calm under pressure. Third, it costs almost nothing. You only need a ball and a friend. To sum up, be patient, be curious and never stop trying. That is my takeaway. And remember the ten-year-old? Last week, I beat her. Thank you for your question: you asked whether you must be good to join. Not at all; beginners are the heart of our club.

Did you know that nine out of ten people who start a book club give up before the third meeting? I almost did. Last year I was a beginner, too shy to speak, and I told myself that nobody wanted my opinion. Today I will show you how I changed my mind. First, I chose a book that I loved, because passion is easier to share than duty. Moreover, I wrote down one question before every meeting. Second, I listened, and having said that, I also learned to disagree politely. Not only did the club improve my reading, but it also gave me the courage to speak in front of strangers. Third, I kept going even when the book was difficult. In conclusion, choose well, prepare one question and stay for the whole evening. That is my message. Good question, by the way: you asked whether you must be a fast reader to join. Not at all; slow readers often say the most interesting things.

answer.text: Thank you, Leo. I take your point, and I agree with you up to a point. Tablets are light, they are cheap to update, and a child can carry a whole library in one bag. But I see one drawback in a complete switch: many pupils read more slowly on a screen, and they get distracted by notifications. For instance, last month my teacher asked us to read a short story on a tablet, and half of the class ended up checking messages. Building on your idea, I would suggest a simple compromise: tablets for research and exercises, and paper for long reading. Furthermore, we could ask pupils to help us write the rules, because people follow what they choose. That is partly why I would not remove paper completely. Mia, what have you noticed with the younger children you work with? Do they read better on paper or on a screen? I would like to hear your view before we decide anything.

origin.text: Ana said that tablets saved time in her classes. Tom replied that he doubted that schools could afford enough of them.

prompt.es: Modera la mesa: presenta, da dos turnos, resume y cierra.

answer.text: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to tonight's panel. Our topic is technology in the classroom. Let me introduce our three panellists: Ana, who uses tablets every day; Tom, who teaches science; and Sara, who has three children at school. Ana, would you like to start? Thank you, Ana. Tom, it is your turn. Sorry to cut in, Tom, but coming back to the main question, could you pin down the cost? Thank you. Before we move on, let me draw the threads together. Ana stressed that tablets saved time. Tom doubted that schools could afford them, and he warned that screens could distract pupils. Sara suggested that we write clear rules, and she conceded that tablets had real benefits. Sara, what would your first rule be? Seldom have I seen three guests agree on so much. To wrap up, all of you agree that rules matter more than machines. I am deeply grateful to each panellist for a lively discussion, and I thank our audience for listening. Good night, everyone.

choices.text: That the authorities make the true figures public.
That schools limit them to a few classrooms.

origin.audio: Near the end of the panel, the moderator summed up: Ana stressed that tablets save time, Tom doubted that schools can afford them, and Sara suggested writing clear rules. Then she asked whether that was a fair summary. Tom nodded, but added that he would support tablets if the council published the real costs. Ana said that she could live with that, and Sara reminded everyone that rules cost nothing. The moderator smiled, thanked all three, and said that, for once, a panel on technology had ended with a plan instead of a quarrel.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige por qué la entrevistadora plantea a veces preguntas tendenciosas.

choices.text: To see whether the candidate accepts a premise or politely challenges it.
To make the candidate feel relaxed before the harder questions begin.
To test whether the candidate has read the course description closely.
To hurry the candidate towards the answer she already expects to hear.

feedback.es: La exentrevistadora dice que lo hace «to see whether a candidate will quietly agree or politely push back»: quiere ver si el candidato acepta la premisa o la discute.

origin.audio: On this week's episode, a former scholarship officer explained what she really listens for. Candidates, she said, prepare for the questions they fear, such as the one about weaknesses, and then stumble over the ones that look simple. Where do you see yourself in five years? sounds like small talk, but it is her way of gauging whether an applicant's ambitions fit the course. She also admitted that she sometimes asks a leading question on purpose, simply to see whether a candidate will quietly agree or politely push back. Silence, she added, costs her nothing, and it often draws out the most honest answers.

prompt.es: ¿Qué sugiere la autora del correo sobre los candidatos de la beca?

choices.text: That hypothetical questions should be dropped because candidates handle them too well.
That polished answers may hide how little some candidates reflect on themselves.
That the applicants have no real limitations worth mentioning to the committee.
That coaching is unfair and should be banned from future scholarship rounds.

feedback.es: La autora deduce que respuestas pulidas pueden decir más del entrenamiento que del carácter; no propone eliminar preguntas ni prohibir nada.

origin.text: Thanks for sitting in on Tuesday's interviews. I noticed that most applicants answered the hypothetical question fluently, yet very few could name a real limitation without rushing to a positive. That may say more about how they were coached than about their character, so I suggest we ask the second kind of question earlier next year.

feedback.es: La nota reconoce que la historia es sólida, pero avisa de que la pregunta era un supuesto y pedía un plan: el fallo es de intención, no de contenido.

origin.text: Feedback note: to the question about funding being cut, the candidate began with “Last year we cut costs”, a solid story, but the committee had asked for a plan. Next time, answer the question that was asked and save the anecdote for the question about challenges.

origin.text: A journalist is preparing written questions for a minister and wants each one to sound polite yet precise.

prompt.es: Escucha el programa y elige qué impresión da la presentadora.

choices.text: Polite in her wording, but happy with a general reply.
Polite in her wording, yet firm about getting a precise answer.
Sharp in her wording, and keen to catch the minister out.
Careful in her wording, though nervous about challenging a senior figure.

feedback.es: Formula peticiones corteses, pero cada vez insiste con una pregunta más precisa y no se conforma con lo general: cortés en la forma, firme en lo que exige.

origin.audio: When the minister described the scheme as a qualified success, the presenter did not move on. Instead, she pressed for detail. To what extent, she asked, did the outcome match the promises made a year earlier? The minister answered that it was too early to say, so she followed up on that: what precisely would count as success? Every indirect request, such as could you tell me what evidence you rely on, was followed by a sharper question. By the end, the minister had been tied to a clear answer without once being interrupted.

prompt.es: ¿Qué propone la editora en este correo y por qué?

choices.text: Rephrasing an accusing question, since the minister has complained about its tone.
Dropping an accusing question, since the information it asks for is not needed.
Rephrasing an accusing question, since the same information can be had more gently.
Keeping the accusing question, but asking it only after the minister has relaxed.

feedback.es: La editora reformula la pregunta como una indirecta cortés: pide lo mismo, pero deja margen para que el ministro explique y no se ponga a la defensiva.

origin.text: Thanks for the draft. Your questions are well researched, but several read like accusations. To what extent did you mislead the public? invites a defensive answer, and the interview may stall. Try Could you tell me how the campaign figures were worked out? It asks for the same information and leaves the minister room to explain.

The third said she had introduced a booking system, and that missed appointments had fallen from thirty a month to eight. The last one claimed that he always exceeded every target, which the coach called a sweeping generalisation, since he gave no example at all. Only one answer, she said, would make an interviewer stop writing and start listening.

origin.audio: Two years ago, I organised a food drive at school. At first, nobody had signed up, so I visited every class and asked each one to choose a captain. As a result, we collected three hundred bags of food in a week. Since then, I have always started with people, not posters, because a poster asks for attention, while a person offers help.

choices.text: That experience taught me that a clear plan matters more than enthusiasm.

That experience has continued for two years without any real change.

feedback.es: «Taught me that…» formula la lección; las otras dos solo aportan información de tiempo, no una enseñanza.

origin.text: An applicant has just told the story of a failed fundraiser and wants to close with one sentence that states clearly what she learned from it.

prompt.es: Escribe tu respuesta: situación, acción, resultado y lección.

answer.text: Two years ago, I was in charge of the school charity concert, which was already in trouble when I took it over. Nobody had booked the hall, the posters had not been printed, and several students had lost interest. I decided to take the initiative. First, I drew up a simple checklist and asked each class to choose a captain who would report to me every Friday. Then I phoned the music teacher, who found us a hall within two days. As a result, we sold every ticket in a week, and the concert has become a yearly tradition since then. The school has raised twice as much money as before. The experience taught me that a clear plan gives people confidence. It was also a hard-won lesson about asking for help early, because the project only began to turn around once I stopped trying to do everything myself. Since then, I have used the same approach in every team I have joined.
accepted: Two years ago, I was in charge of the school charity concert, which was already in trouble when I took it over. As a result, we sold every ticket in a week, and the concert has become a yearly tradition since then. The school has raised twice as much money as before. The experience taught me that a clear plan gives people confidence. It was also a hard-won lesson about asking for help early, because the project only began to turn around once I stopped trying to do everything myself. Since then, I have used the same approach in every team I have joined.

Last year, I was in charge of the school garden. When I joined, nobody had watered the plants for a month, and most of the volunteers had already stopped coming. I decided to start again with a clear plan. I made a watering rota, I asked each class to choose a captain and I called the science teacher to ask for help. Within a week, the garden looked alive again. As a result, it has produced vegetables every summer since then, and the canteen has used them in its menu. The experience taught me that people help when they know exactly what they have to do. I also learned that asking for support early saves a lot of time. Today I use the same method whenever I start a new project.

feedback.es: Una respuesta completa sitúa la historia, recuerda un hecho anterior, cuenta tu acción, da un resultado que sigue vigente y cierra con una lección.

origin.text: En una entrevista para un programa de liderazgo te piden: «Cuéntame una ocasión en que lideraste un proyecto que iba mal». Escribe 210–270 palabras: situación y acción en pasado, un hecho anterior con pasado perfecto, un resultado vigente con presente perfecto y la lección aprendida.

prompt.es: Escucha el relato y elige qué da a entender su última respuesta sobre el liderazgo.

origin.audio: During a scholarship interview, a candidate was asked about a time when she had led a team. She listened to both, drew up a shared plan and gave each group its own captain. The campaign has collected more rubbish every year since then. Asked what she had learned, she answered that a leader's first job is to make sure everyone knows who is responsible for what.

answer.text: Thanks for having me. I am delighted to be your guest today. You asked what led me to start the repair café. Briefly, it began two years ago, when I noticed that my neighbours threw away broken toasters and lamps every week. When I arrived at the first meeting, nobody had brought any tools, so I drew up a short list, asked each volunteer to bring one item and borrowed a table from the library. As a result, we have repaired more than two hundred objects since then. You also asked about my biggest challenge. Honestly, it was persuading people to open up about what they could not fix. For example, in March only six neighbours came, but after I wrote a simple invitation, attendance rose from six to thirty. If I may turn that around, to what extent do your listeners already repair things at home? To wrap up, if there is one key takeaway for the listeners, it is this: start small, and ask for help early. The experience taught me that people will share skills if someone makes the first move. Thank you again for the invitation.

origin.audio: In his review of the podcast, the critic praised the guest for her preparation. She opened warmly, answered each question with a short story and never wasted a sentence. What impressed him most, however, came at the end. When the host pressed her on the weakest part of her project, she did not hide behind general phrases. She conceded a fair point, opened up about what had gone wrong and then turned the question around, asking the host how listeners usually respond to failure. The critic admitted that he had expected a polished sales pitch, and that he had been quietly won over instead.

origin.audio: On the show, a speaking coach described three ways to buy time and ranked them by register. Hang on, she said, works among friends but sounds curt in a formal meeting. That's a tricky question is neutral, and useful because it flatters the questioner while you think. Allow me a moment to consider that is the most formal, yet it carries a risk: if the pause that follows is too long, politeness turns into anxiety. Her advice was to combine two of them, naming the difficulty and then thinking out loud, because listeners forgive a pause far more easily than they forgive an empty reply.

answer.text: That's a tricky one, so let me think for a second. My stance is that a generalist has more options than a specialist. The main reason is that jobs change faster than any single specialist can follow. A generalist can move between fields, learn new tools and adapt when a company changes direction. For example, my cousin trained as a nurse, then worked in a hospital office, and now manages a small clinic. If she had stayed only a specialist, she would not have had those chances. Of course, specialists are important, and I would not want a generalist to be my doctor. Sorry, I'm rambling a little; let me get back to my point. So, in short, I would rather be a generalist with one strong skill, because that mix gives me both skill and choices.
