Let me think for a moment. I would say that specialists are better, so my stance is clear. The first reason is that experts solve hard problems faster. A specialist has spent years on one subject, and companies pay more for that skill. For example, my uncle is an engineer who only repairs bridges, and he is always busy because nobody else can do his job. Some people say that a generalist is more flexible, and that is true. However, I think being flexible without real skill is risky, because a generalist may never learn anything well. That is why I prefer to commit to one field and to learn it thoroughly. To sum up, I believe that a specialist has the advantage, and I would advise young people to choose one area and to become really good at it.

origin.audio: After the timer stopped, the coach played back a student's answer. The student had begun well: a short pause, then a clear stance on whether the school day should start later. But with ten seconds left she remembered a second example and began telling it, and the minute ended before she could close. The coach did not question the content. She pointed at the clock and said that an answer without a closing sentence is like a story without its last line.

prompt.es: Escribe una crítica matizada de la publicación (220–280 palabras).

answer.text: The post makes an interesting point, but I think its conclusion needs more care. First, the writer seems to overlook the size of the sample: only thirty pupils from one class were asked, so the result may fall short of what a general claim requires. Second, the post rests on the idea that headphones stop fights, but it gives no evidence of how the fights were counted, which leaves the method open to question. To some extent, the fall in fights is likely to be linked to the headphones, although other factors, such as the weather or a new teacher, may also account for it. Arguably, the pupils who use headphones are simply the quiet ones, so the link is tenuous. Rather than handing out headphones in every school, a reasonable alternative would be to survey several classes for a whole term and compare the results. A balanced critique must also admit that the idea is worth testing, and I would certainly support a careful trial.

To begin with, the writer seems to overlook how small the sample was: thirty pupils from a single class cannot speak for a whole school, so the evidence falls short of a general rule. Besides, the post never explains how the fights were counted, and that raises doubts about the method. answer.text: Our check of the viral story gives a mixed picture. First, the video seems genuine, but it has no date and no original source, so it was probably shared out of context, and we rate the claim that it shows a secret payment as unproven. Second, the council says that the envelope was a gift for a school, and nobody has confirmed the blogger's version, which comes from an anonymous source. Third, the official figures confirm that the parks budget fell by twelve per cent, so that claim is true, although the fall is not necessarily linked to the video. What is missing is hard evidence: a dated recording, the receipt for the gift and a statement from the people who were there. It is arguably unfair to blame the mayor, and it would be reasonable to wait for more evidence before we share the story.

Nevertheless, the new school offered music lessons that my old school did not, so I made up my mind and moved. The first weeks were difficult, because nobody knew me and the timetable was confusing. Even so, I soon joined the choir, and I am happy with my decision today. My parents now say that the move changed my life, and my old friends often visit me. answer.text: I will argue that the school should not ban phones at break, because a ban solves the wrong problem. First, pupils use their phones to talk to friends who are in other classes, and this contact is the only chance they have to do so. Second, a ban teaches pupils to hide their phones instead of using them well. Last term, for example, my class agreed on a simple rule and complaints fell by half. Admittedly, some pupils spend the whole break looking at a screen. Nevertheless, this is a problem of habits, not of phones, and, as mentioned above, a rule that pupils help to write is easier to respect. Some teachers take issue with this view, but a sensible alternative would be phone-free zones, which persuade without pushing anybody. I also believe that the school should trust us more, because trust is the best way to teach responsibility. In conclusion, the school should give us a say and trust us to use our phones well. Nevertheless, this is a problem of habits, not of phones, and, as mentioned above, a rule that pupils help to write is easier to respect. Some teachers take issue with this view, but a sensible alternative would be phone-free zones, which persuade without pushing anybody. In my opinion, the school should not take phones away at break, because a ban would hurt pupils who use them sensibly. First, many of us talk to friends from other classes, and this is often our only chance to do so. Second, a strict rule would teach us to hide our phones rather than to control them. Last year, for instance, our class made its own rule, and arguments about phones almost disappeared. It is true that some pupils stare at a screen for the whole break. Even so, this is a question of habits, and, as noted above, rules that pupils help to write are easier to respect. A reasonable alternative would be quiet zones, where phones are allowed only for messages. Some teachers take issue with this view, but I think it is fair to ask them for trust. In short, pupils deserve a say in this decision, and the magazine should keep asking for it. Revision: I trimmed two long sentences and removed a repeated example.

answer.text: Our survey of two hundred pupils produced two main findings. First, sixty per cent of the pupils sleep less than eight hours a night. Second, among those who sleep little, twice as many girls as boys say that they feel tired in class. These figures suggest that a lack of sleep may affect how pupils feel at school, and they appear to show that girls are more affected than boys, at least to some extent. However, the results have an important limitation. All the pupils came from one school, and they described their own sleep, so the data may not be reliable. For this reason, we cannot say that sleep causes tiredness; we can only say that the two seem to be linked. Further research with a larger sample from several schools would be needed before anyone could generalise these results to all teenagers. We therefore treat them as a starting point, not as proof. In short, the findings stand out and deserve attention, but they should be read with caution.
accepted: Our survey of two hundred pupils produced two main findings. First, sixty per cent of the pupils sleep less than eight hours a night. We asked two hundred pupils about their sleep and found two things that stand out. To begin with, 60 per cent of them sleep for less than eight hours a night. In addition, among the pupils who sleep little, double the number of girls compared with boys reported feeling tired during lessons. The data indicate that a lack of sleep could affect how pupils feel at school, and girls seem to be more affected than boys to some extent. Nevertheless, there is a key limitation: only one school took part, and the pupils reported their own hours, so the answers may not be reliable. Because of this, the results do not show that sleep causes tiredness; they only point to a link. Further research with a larger sample from different schools would help us to see whether the same pattern appears elsewhere, and whether anyone can generalise from it. We therefore see them as a starting point, not as proof. To sum up, the findings are useful, but they must be treated with caution.

answer.text: Last June a survey was conducted among three hundred residents of the old neighbourhood. The participants were selected at random from a list and were asked to complete a questionnaire online. Two results stand out. First, roughly a third of the residents said that the street lighting is poor, whereas the vast majority praised the park. Second, twice as many older residents as young ones feel unsafe at night. These findings suggest that lighting may be a top priority for the neighbourhood, and they appear to show that older people are more worried. However, there is an important limitation: most answers came from two streets, and the residents described their own feelings, so the data may be biased. For that reason, we cannot generalise the results to the whole city. As a next step, we propose a three-month trial run of new lamps in the two streets, and we suggest that the council should report the results in the autumn. Further research with a larger sample would then show whether the change really helped, and whether residents in other streets feel the same way.
accepted: Last June a survey was conducted among three hundred residents of the old neighbourhood. However, there is an important limitation: most answers came from two streets, and the residents described their own feelings, so the data may be biased. We conducted a survey in June, and three hundred residents of the old town answered an online questionnaire. They were chosen at random from a local list. We found two main things. To begin with, about a third of the residents think the street lighting is poor, while the vast majority like the park. In addition, double the number of older people compared with young people feel unsafe when they walk at night. This indicates that better lighting could be a top priority, and it seems that older residents are more concerned. Nevertheless, there is a limitation. Most of the answers came from two streets, and people only reported how they feel, so the results may not be reliable. We therefore cannot say that the same is true for the whole city. Our proposal is a trial run of three months with new lamps in those streets, and we recommend that the council reports the results in the autumn. More research with a larger sample would show whether the trial helped and whether people in other streets feel the same.

feedback.es: El texto resume el método en pasivo, da resultados con proporciones, usa verbos cautos, explica un límite y propone un paso siguiente.

origin.text: Encuesta vecinal (junio): 300 residentes del barrio antiguo, elegidos al azar de una lista, respondieron un cuestionario en línea. Límite: respondieron sobre todo vecinos de dos calles y los datos son declarados. Propuesta: una prueba de tres meses con farolas nuevas y un informe del municipio. origin.text: Dear Councillor, I write on behalf of the residents of Mill Lane. Our survey, completed by two hundred and forty neighbours, found that nearly a third consider the street lighting poor, whereas most are satisfied with the park. We accept that the answers came mainly from two streets, and we do not claim to speak for the whole neighbourhood. Nevertheless, twice as many residents over sixty as under thirty told us that they no longer walk home after dark. We ask the council to consider a trial run of brighter lamps in our street, and we would be glad to help to monitor the results.

origin.audio: Four flatmates were planning a surprise party, and nobody finished a sentence. Mia laughed, said hang on, as she was saying, the cake came first, and asked Sara to go ahead. Sara repeated the date, and everyone agreed, although Carlos was still not sure about the money.

origin.audio: Last month I joined a project with colleagues in four countries, and the first call was a lesson in listening. Ana, in Pune, asked whether we could prepone the next meeting to nine o'clock, and for a moment I thought she meant the opposite. Leo, in Lagos, opened with how far, which is simply hello, and promised to flash me when he arrived, because a proper call would eat up his credit. Mia, in Cork, said that she was grand, just after finishing her exams. Finally Tom, in Perth, reckoned there would be heaps of time this arvo. None of it was difficult once I stopped working out every word and started to get the gist.

answer.text: The lecturer began by saying that she wanted to look at why some companies are trying a four-day working week, and she then outlined three main reasons. According to her, the first reason is that staff are more focused when a long weekend is coming, and the work done stayed the same at one firm in Bristol. The second reason is that sick days fell sharply, by about a third in a year. The third reason is that it became easier to recruit, because candidates see the shorter week as a sign of trust. By way of illustration, she described a company that reduced its hours from forty to thirty-two without cutting pay. She went on to draw attention to a limit: the change is not suitable for every kind of business, since hospitals and shops cannot simply close on Fridays. In short, the lecturer said that the four-day week works best where results, not hours, can be measured, and she did not suggest that every company should copy it.

origin.audio: Good morning. Today I want to look at why some companies are trying a four-day working week. There are three main reasons. Second, sick days fell sharply, by about a third in a year. Third, it became easier to recruit, because candidates see the shorter week as a sign of trust. By way of illustration, one company reduced its hours from forty to thirty-two without cutting pay. However, the change is not suitable for every kind of business; hospitals and shops cannot simply close on Fridays. In short, the four-day week works best where results can be measured, not hours.

prompt.es: Escucha el episodio y escribe un resumen con una implicación y tu reacción.

answer.text: In this episode, the host asked her guest, a researcher, whether it is better to work from home. According to the guest, it depends. First, many people save about two hours a day because they no longer travel, and she called this a real benefit. Second, she said that some people feel lonely and hardly see their colleagues. Third, she suggested that companies could offer two office days a week, which she described as a fair compromise. When the host asked whether working at home is better, she answered that it is not exactly better, which seemed to imply that the answer is not a simple yes. What struck me was that she never said it is easy. To be fair, I found the episode balanced, and I see her point about the benefits. However, I would add one doubt of my own: two office days a week may be hard to organise for small firms, so the compromise may suit large companies better. My gut reaction was to agree with her up to a point. In short, the episode was clear and useful, and I would like to hear how companies respond.

This episode of the podcast was about working from home. The host asked her guest whether it is better, and the guest explained that it depends. On the positive side, many people save two hours a day because they no longer travel to an office. On the negative side, some of them feel lonely and hardly see their colleagues. She suggested that a good compromise could be two office days a week. The host asked again whether working at home is better, and the guest replied not exactly, which implied that the situation is more complicated than a simple yes or no. My reaction is positive: to be fair, she did not try to sell one answer, and what struck me was how honest she was about the problems. However, I would add that two office days a week could be hard to organise for small firms, and that could make the compromise less useful for them. Overall, I agree with her up to a point, and I would like to hear how companies respond to her ideas.

origin.audio: In this week's episode, the host asked her guest, a researcher who studies remote work, whether working from home is better. The guest said that it depends. Many people, she explained, save about two hours a day because they no longer travel, and that is a real benefit. Asked whether it is therefore better, she answered: not exactly. Some people told her that they feel lonely and hardly see their colleagues. The host asked whether there is a solution, and the guest suggested, after a slight pause, that companies could offer two office days a week, which she called a fair compromise. She added that not everyone has a quiet room at home, a point that she said is often overlooked. The host thanked her and promised to return to the subject.

The other eight are different. Three times she wrote the increase of prices, twice she added but after much as, and three times she opened a request with a direct question. origin.audio: When we drafted our style guide last spring, several of us argued for a single pattern, and I was one of them. The guide now says that every contingency clause must begin with should, and I still see the logic: the pattern is short and formal. In an email to a colleague, though, Should it rain, the match will be postponed can sound stiff. I would keep the rule for contracts and reports, and leave emails free to use a plain if. Asking every reader to accept one pattern would only make our writing less natural. Having tested it on real emails, I have changed my mind.

origin.audio: The final verse of Last Bus Home is only four lines long. The singer folds a timetable into her pocket, turns off the hall light and says, to the empty hall, that some doors are better left unlocked. Nothing in the verse mentions the person who left. Critics have noticed that the word tomorrow appears in every verse except this one, and that its absence makes the ending feel quieter, less hopeful and more final. Yet the unlocked door suggests that the singer has not entirely given up. It is, the host concludes, a song that refuses to explain itself, and that is exactly why people keep arguing about it.

answer.text: Rain tapped the window of the night bus. Tom counted his coins twice, and then a third time, while his foot beat the floor. Behind him, a man in a grey suit sighed at his own watch. On Tom's knees lay the folder with his drawings, and his hands would not stay still. The driver hummed a cheerful song, which made everything worse. Off the bus he jumped, and up the stairs he ran. Silence in the corridor. A closed door. He was sure he had missed the interview by ten minutes, and he had practised his speech all week. Then a woman appeared at the end of the hall, holding a cup of tea. "Are you Tom?" she asked. "We had to postpone everything. The director, of course, is stuck in traffic." Tom laughed so loudly that the secretary looked up. It turned out that the director had been sitting behind him on the bus all along, and he arrived five minutes later, out of breath, blaming the driver's song. In the end, Tom got the job, and the driver got a thank-you card.

Every Sunday my grandfather fished at the lake, and every Sunday he came home with an empty bucket and a happy face. My mother laughed and said that fishing was only an excuse to sit in silence. One morning I followed him. Into the water went his line, and out of the silence came nothing. Hours passed. Nobody spoke, and even the gulls seemed to be waiting for something to happen. The lake stayed as still as a painting. Then a tiny silver fish jumped into the bucket by itself. My grandfather stared at it. His hands shook a little as he lifted the bucket. I had never seen him so excited, or so suspicious. "Of course," he said at last, "the day I bring a friend, the fish behave." It turned out that he had been hiding a secret all along: he had never caught a single fish, and he was delighted about it. In the end, he let the fish go and told everybody it was the best catch of his life. Since then, he has never fished alone.

answer.text: I would like to put forward a proposal for the open day: a story workshop in the square. By last spring, the square had been empty for months, and many neighbours told me they missed a place to meet. A workshop with a small book stall could change that. The square belongs to all of us, and a story is the cheapest way to fill it. I know that a new idea always raises questions, and I welcome them, because a fair point can only improve the plan. I understand that the budget is tight, and much as I appreciate your concern, I believe we can manage. I was wondering whether the volunteers could bring the books and the chairs, so the cost would be almost nothing, and nobody would need to spend money on anything else. Should it rain, we will move the workshop into the hall. Failing that, we can shorten the morning. If everyone agrees, I will confirm the stall by Friday, and by Saturday we will have prepared the posters. Shall we agree on that? Thank you for listening, and I hope you will join us.

Let me put forward a proposal: a story workshop for the open day. When I was a child, the square used to be full of people, and I would love to see that again. Stories can bring neighbours together, and a simple workshop is a good way to start. I also believe that a workshop like this costs very little and gives a lot back. Nobody needs a big stage to tell a story, only a few chairs and a little time. Fair enough, the budget is limited. Much as I would like a bigger stall, I am sure the volunteers can help, and I was wondering whether the library could lend us some books for the morning. In the event of rain, the workshop will take place in the hall. By Friday I will have confirmed the stall with the council, and the posters will be ready by Saturday. That is our deadline, and I am confident that we can meet it together. Are we all happy with this plan? Thank you for listening, and I hope that many of you will come and tell a story of your own.

I would like to propose a workshop where neighbours write a short story together, one sentence each. The idea came from last year, when a stranger left a notebook on a bench and within a week the whole street had filled it. I understand that some of you worry about the noise and the cost, and I accept that both are fair points. Much as I am keen on the idea, I would not want it to divide us. I was wondering whether we could try it for one morning, with a small stall and a handful of volunteers, and then decide. Should the weather turn bad, we can use the library. By Friday I will have spoken to the volunteers, and by the following Friday we will have a clear answer. If the morning goes badly, at least we will have tried. I am not asking for a big budget, only for one morning and a little goodwill from all of us. Does that seem a fair compromise? Thank you for listening, and please tell me what you think before we vote.

answer.text: I would argue that a city should close its centre to cars, at least on weekends and in the busiest streets. Take my own town: two years ago the main square was full of traffic, and the shopkeepers used to complain that nobody could stop to look at the windows. Once the square became pedestrian, the shops gradually received more visitors, and the noise dropped noticeably. Admittedly, a ban is not free of problems, because older residents may find it harder to reach the centre and some deliveries may arrive late. Much as I accept that risk, I believe it is smaller than it looks, since a free bus and a few parking spaces at the edge can cover most needs. Or rather, it is smaller when the council consults the residents in advance. What I mean is that the plan hinges on preparation, not on enthusiasm. Every choice has a downside, but this one can sway even a sceptical shopkeeper if the trial is honest and limited. On balance, I would propose a six-month experiment, and I would revise the decision calmly once the figures are in.
accepted: I would argue that a city should close its centre to cars, at least on weekends and in the busiest streets. Take my own town: two years ago the main square was full of traffic, and the shopkeepers used to complain that nobody could stop to look at the windows. Once the square became pedestrian, the shops gradually received more visitors, and the noise dropped noticeably. Admittedly, a ban is not free of problems, because older residents may find it harder to reach the centre and some deliveries may arrive late. Much as I accept that risk, I believe it is smaller than it looks, since a free bus and a few parking spaces at the edge can cover most needs. Or rather, it is smaller when the council consults the residents in advance. What I mean is that the plan hinges on preparation, not on enthusiasm. Every choice has a downside, but this one can sway even a sceptical shopkeeper if the trial is honest and limited. On balance, I would propose a six-month experiment, and I would revise the decision calmly once the figures are in.

In my opinion, closing the city centre to cars is worth a serious trial, especially on the streets where people already walk more than they drive. Consider my aunt's bakery: two years ago the customers used to complain about the noise, and the drivers would park in front of the door for an hour. After the street became pedestrian, the bakery sold more, and the pavement was full of families. It is true that a few elderly customers were unhappy at first, because they could not get close by car. Even though that problem is real, I think it is easy to solve with a free bus and a few parking spaces nearby. To put it more precisely, the real difficulty is not the missing road but the lack of preparation. Let me rephrase that: a car-free centre works only when everyone knows how to arrive. Admittedly, not every street can be closed, and a hospital cannot be cut off. Still, many centres could. All in all, the evidence I have seen points to a modest but clear benefit, and I would support a trial.

answer.text: Years ago, I used to believe that I would never speak English well. I had never spoken with a stranger in English, and I was afraid of making mistakes. Then I started studying with an app every morning, and in hindsight that routine was the start of my journey. The article says that students who learn with apps never speak fluently. Admittedly, an app alone may not be enough: it cannot give you a real conversation. Much as I respect the author, I would argue that the claim is too strong. The source seems to rely on a small survey, and its evidence looks anecdotal, so its conclusion may not be reliable. I was wondering whether the author could explain how many students took part. I understand that a short article has little space, and I appreciate the concern about speaking well. Revision: I first wrote that apps are useless for speaking, or rather, I should say that they are useful but not enough. On balance, the best plan is an app plus real conversations, and that is exactly what this course has given me, so I feel confident now.

When I was a child, I would watch films in English without understanding a word, and my cousin used to laugh at me. Later, I had to take an exam, and that was the moment when I decided to learn properly. An online post claims that apps are a waste of time and that nobody learns to speak with them. It is true that an app cannot replace a teacher. Even though I agree with part of that view, I think the post may be wrong, because it gives no numbers and does not say who wrote it.
